title: Trick or Treat? The Impact of Employment Protection Laws (EPLs) on Employee Welfare
affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University - School of Accounting and Finance, Hong Kong Polytechnic University - School of Accounting and Finance, Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Capital University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Trick or Treat? The Impact of Employment Protection Laws (EPLs) on Employee Welfare
detail.abstract: How would employers treat their employees when terminating employment became more difficult? To investigate this question, we exploit changes in employment protection laws (EPLs) across 37 countries and examine the impact of these laws on employee welfare. We find that employee welfare improves following the implementation of more stringent EPLs, suggesting that enhanced stringency of employment protection incentivizes employers to pay closer attention to the welfare of their incumbent employees to elicit greater employee effort and commitment. Further tests show that EPLs improve employee compensation, encourage the provision of high-quality employment benefits, and reduce employee turnover. The positive effects of EPLs on employee welfare are more pronounced in labor-intensive industries and in developing economies. Finally, we show that improvements in employee welfare enhance both firm value and productivity.

affiliations: Macquarie University, Monash University and

detail.title: Corporate Culture and Climate-Related Disclosure Informativeness
detail.abstract: This study examines whether and how corporate culture affects the informativeness of climate-related disclosures. We conceptualize disclosure informativeness as an information-efficiency outcome, which captures the extent to which climate risk disclosures convey decision-relevant information with minimal redundancy and processing cost. To operationalize this construct, we use large language models to generate firm-specific, information-efficient summaries of climate risk disclosures and calculate the ratio of the summary length to original disclosure length. Based on U.S. firms from 2005 to 2020, we find that strong corporate culture is associated with more informative climate disclosures. Mechanism analyses suggest that strong-culture firms have better climate performance and greater internal climate reporting capacity. The association is stronger when formal governance and external monitoring are weaker and information asymmetry is higher, consistent with culture serving as an informal substitute governance mechanism. Overall, our findings identify corporate culture as an important internal determinant of climate disclosure informativeness.

title: KYS: Know Your Swarm and the Fairness Layer: Interaction-Mediated Proxy Discrimination in Multi-Agent and Interacting Systems

detail.abstract:
Much of algorithmic fairness research and assurance evaluates fairness at the level of the individual model, decision rule or automated system. The emergence of agentic and multi-agent architectures unsettles that unit of analysis. Consequential outcomes may instead be produced through interactions among specialised agents that gather information, interpret context, assess risk, route decisions and act on one another's outputs. This paper deepens a fairness strand already present in the KYS: Know Your Swarm research programme, moving from earlier work on swarm-level bias and collective-system fairness to the more specific problem of discrimination produced through interactions among multiple agents.


It introduces interaction-mediated proxy discrimination as the umbrella phenomenon: a process through which information correlated with a protected characteristic acquires, preserves, changes or intensifies discriminatory significance as it is transmitted, interpreted, transformed, reconstructed, routed, thresholded or acted upon across interacting agents, even where no individual agent independently produces an equivalent discriminatory outcome. The contribution is not to claim that proxy discrimination, non-compositional fairness, sequential effects or emergent multi-agent bias are new, but to make the cross-agent lineage of proxy-relevant information a primary analytical object and connect it to the interaction-governance architecture established in earlier KYS work.


Building on the author's earlier treatment of swarm-level bias and inclusion (Usman Chaudhry 2026a), and the subsequent development of collective-system fairness, proxy propagation and adaptive disadvantage (Usman Chaudhry 2026c), the paper develops a more specific account of how proxy-relevant information becomes consequential across interacting agents. It distinguishes semantic proxy transformation, proxy reconstruction and routing-mediated disparity as interaction-level mechanisms, while incorporating established cumulative, contextual and feedback dynamics.


The paper argues that fairness assurance must operate not only on model outputs but also on the identity, delegated authority, interaction provenance, intervention points and institutional responsibility associated with the composite decision. The five KYS pillars - Agent Identity, Authorized Intent, Interaction Mapping, Human Override and Accountable Redress - remain unchanged; the paper develops their application to interaction-level fairness.


Autonomous Finance, particularly credit, provides the primary worked case because financial decisions directly shape economic participation and financial governance already imposes institutional accountability. The interaction-layer principle is then applied to other complex interacting systems, including platform ecosystems and technology-facilitated gender-based violence, public services and hiring. Gender bias is treated as a stress test for whether interaction-level governance can identify harms distributed across individually compliant components. The argument is anticipatory: the architectures capable of producing such failures are emerging now, creating an opportunity to establish interaction-level governance before they become embedded in consequential infrastructure.

תקציר בעברית: מחקר השוואתי זה בוחן את המסגרות הרגולטוריות והחקיקתיות המתפתחות המסדירות נתונים ביומטריים וטכנולוגיות זיהוי פנים (FRT) במדינות חברות נבחרות באיחוד האירופי ובאוסטרליה. המחקר בוחן כיצד תחומי שיפוט משפטיים שונים מאזנים בין מטרות של האינטרס הציבורי - כולל אכיפת חוק, ביטחון לאומי, בריאות הציבור ויעילות אדמיניסטרטיבית - לבין הציווי להגן על פרטיות אישית, כבוד האדם, זכויות דמוקרטיות בסיסיות ואבטחת מידע. 

 הדו"ח מתמקד במקורות נורמטיביים ראשוניים, בעיקר תקנת הגנת המידע הכללית של האיחוד האירופי (GDPR), הוראת אכיפת החוק (LED) וחוק הבינה המלאכותית של האיחוד האירופי (AI Act), לצד חקיקה לאומית רלוונטית בתחומי שיפוט כמו גרמניה, איטליה, אירלנד, בלגיה, בולגריה, דנמרק, אסטוניה, יוון ואוסטרליה.

  ממצאים מבניים מרכזיים של הניתוח ההשוואתי כוללים: 
1. מעבר למודל רחב מבוסס סיכונים: רגולציה מודרנית עוברת מהגנה מסורתית על הפרטיות (מניעת דליפות נתונים אישיים) למסגרת רחבה יותר של ניהול סיכונים. מסגרת זו מכוונת לסיכונים חברתיים ודמוקרטיים מערכתיים, כולל אפליה אלגוריתמית, הדרה חברתית, אובדן אוטונומיה אישית, השפעות מצמררות על חירויות הציבור, זיהוי שגוי וחוסר איזון מבני בכוח. 

2. עקרונות הכרחיות ומידתיות מחמירים: יעילות תפעולית או נוחות אדמיניסטרטיבית בלבד אינם מצדיקים עוד עיבוד ביומטרי. זיהוי ביומטרי נחשב כאמצעי חריג, המותר רק כאשר הוא הכרחי לחלוטין למטרה לגיטימית ומשכנעת, וכאשר חלופות פחות פולשניות אינן זמינות. 

3. הגנה מורחבת לאוכלוסיות פגיעות: אמצעי הגנה רגולטוריים מתרחבים מעבר לקטינים וכוללים עובדים (עקב אסימטריה של כוח במקום העבודה), סטודנטים, אנשים עם מוגבלויות פיזיות או קוגניטיביות, קבוצות מוחלשות מבחינה סוציו-אקונומית, קורבנות פשע, עדים מוגנים ואנשים שנפטרו. 

4. הגבלות מחמירות על טכנולוגיות זיהוי פנים (FRT): במסגרת חוק הבינה המלאכותית של האיחוד האירופי וחקיקה לאומית, יישומים בסיכון גבוה של FRT עומדים בפני הגבלות חמורות. אלה כוללים איסורים על זיהוי ביומטרי מרחוק בזמן אמת במרחבים נגישים לציבור (בכפוף לחריגים צרים של אכיפת החוק), גירוד תמונות לא ממוקד ברשת לבניית מאגרי מידע לזיהוי, סיווג ביומטרי המבוסס על מאפיינים רגישים וניקוד חברתי. 

5. ניהול סיכונים פרואקטיבי ומזעור נתונים: פרדיגמות רגולטוריות מעדיפות מזעור נתונים ופתרונות אחסון מבוזרים או מקומיים על פני מאגרי מידע לאומיים רחבים ומרכזיים. גופים המשתמשים במערכות ביומטריות חייבים ליישם אמצעי תאימות פרואקטיביים, כולל הערכות השפעות הגנת נתונים (DPIA), קציני הגנת נתונים (DPO) ורישום גישה חובה. 

6. פיקוח מוגבר ועונשים חמורים: לרשויות הגנת נתונים עצמאיות (DPA) ולרשויות מעקב שוק יש סמכויות חקירה ואכיפה מורחבות. אי ציות מגובה בקנסות מנהליים חמורים לצד אחריות פלילית פוטנציאלית בתחומי שיפוט ספציפיים.

Both problems are easy, because pessimist and optimist alikebehave as if the world were riskless. A realist, responding optimally to risk,spends between the two. title: Can Educational Policies Reduce Wealth Inequality?
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Innovation and Competition

detail.title: Can Educational Policies Reduce Wealth Inequality?
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between education and wealth accumulation using U.S. panel data spanning two generations. Employing multiple identification strategies, the analysis finds that educational attainment significantly increases lifetime wealth, with particularly strong effects for college and postgraduate education. Building on these empirical results, the paper develops and calibrates a life-cycle heterogeneous-agent model to evaluate how educational policies shape the distribution of wealth. The model simulates two policies: expanding access to higher education and improving education quality. These simulations show that increasing college attainment reduces wealth inequality by broadening access to high-return educational investments. In contrast, improvements in education quality raise productivity and returns among college graduates but may increase wealth inequality when gains accrue disproportionately to already advantaged individuals. The results highlight education’s dual role in promoting economic mobility and shaping wealth inequality.

title: "Rural Resilience: Analyzing the Socio-Economic Challenges of Flood-Induced Displacement in Coastal Bangladesh"
affiliations: Assistant Professor ( Sociology) Southeast University, Bangladesh

detail.title: "Rural Resilience: Analyzing the Socio-Economic Challenges of Flood-Induced Displacement in Coastal Bangladesh"
detail.abstract: Coastal Bangladeshis are vulnerable to seasonal flooding and consequent temporary displacement, with adverse implications for their socio-economic well-being and rural inequality. However, disaster management policies are currently dominated by technocratic approaches, and there is a need to understand how environmental displacement affects informal social resources and capital. This paper aims to assess the social and economic impacts of seasonal flood-induced displacement on vulnerable groups. The study employed a descriptive qualitative design, and data was gathered through ten focus group discussions (FGDs, N=88) conducted in Satkhira, Khulna, and Bhola districts among small-scale farmers, landless laborers, female-headed households, boat owners, and local authorities. The analysis was guided by the conceptual framework of climate vulnerability, adaptive capacity, and informal support systems. The results uncovered four key issues, namely the depletion of agricultural labor force, informal money lenders’ dominance, absence of gender-segregated shelters, and elite dominance in aid distribution. The findings revealed that seasonal flooding causes significant disruptions to agricultural labor, forcing many households into taking high-interest private loans. and the absence of gender-segregated shelters increases the risks of sexual violence and reproductive health problems for women and children. Besides, the research discovered the role of patronage in climate change adaptation and disaster management in costal population. Overall, this paper demonstrates that climate-induced displacement is a significant social determinant of health and economic insecurity, especially among vulnerable groups. As such, there is a need for gender-responsive and social protection policies in climate change adaptation and disaster management policies in coastal developing countries.

title: Marital Endowments and Mental Health: Evidence from South Asia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Marital Endowments and Mental Health: Evidence from South Asia
detail.abstract: This paper studies the effect of dowries on women’s mental health by using international gold price fluctuations at marriage as a source of exogenous variation. In South Asia, gold jewelry is a central part of dowry, and changes in gold prices influence the value of the dowry under a woman's control. Using data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) in Nepal, I find that higher gold prices at the time of marriage are associated with lower anxiety (GAD-7) and depression (PHQ-9) scores later in life. A 10% increase in gold prices at the time of marriage leads to a 0.134-point drop in anxiety and a 0.197-point drop in depression, amounting to 3.9% and 7.2% declines relative to their respective sample means. These results are robust to the inclusion of a battery of controls and hold qualitatively across different specifications. While exploring mechanisms, I provide evidence that higher gold prices at the time of marriage lead to reduced domestic violence, better treatment at home, marginal improvements in women's decision-making power, and no discernible changes in match quality. The effects are marginally stronger among older women, those with secondary education, and those living in nuclear households. As a robustness check, I find similar results in other South Asian countries where dowries are common. As a placebo, I find no effect of gold prices in African countries, which do not have a dowry tradition. Taken together, the findings suggest that initial marital endowments have lasting consequences for women’s mental well-being.

detail.title: Measurement-quality vulnerability in AI-assisted spirometry: a within-participant reliability evaluation of two released models
detail.abstract: Background and objective: Spirometry is effort dependent, and technically degraded maneuvers may remain processable by disease-oriented artificial intelligence (AI). We examined whether maneuver quality changes AI outputs within participants, whether the released outputs reveal that change, and how representation analysis informs reliability assessment before deployment.Methods: We evaluated frozen DeepSpiro and Google ML-COPD models without retraining on 38,044 pre-bronchodilator maneuvers from 8,399 adults in NHANES 2007–2012. Representation analyses used participant-disjoint development (n = 1,685) and confirmatory (n = 6,714) subsets. The primary paired analysis compared the first eligible A/B and C/D maneuvers in 2,951 confirmatory participants. Endpoints included paired output discrepancy, model-specific category or threshold changes, and quality discrimination from released outputs and latent representations. We also assessed simple acquisition proxies, retained physiological information, and rank-1 removal of a quality-associated direction.Results: Mean absolute paired output discrepancy was 0.0369 for DeepSpiro and 0.0312 for Google ML-COPD. Model-specific state changes occurred in 289/2,951 DeepSpiro pairs (9.8%) and 831/2,951 Google pairs (28.2%). These definitions were operational rather than clinical error rates. Final outputs weakly discriminated C/D from A/B maneuvers (AUROC, 0.543 and 0.582), whereas latent representations achieved AUROCs of 0.932 and 0.788. A duration/order/acceptability baseline reached 0.833, below DeepSpiro latent discrimination but above Google latent discrimination. Physiology AUROC was 0.809 and 0.794 before removal and fell by 0.0160 and 0.0132 after removal, respectively. Output instability changed little.Conclusions: Lower-quality maneuvers introduced within-participant operational variation that was weakly reflected in the released disease-oriented outputs. Internal quality-related information differed between models, and removing one linear direction did not improve robustness while modestly reducing physiological decodability. Quality control should therefore be evaluated alongside disease prediction when AI is assessed for spirometry use.

title: Dynamic AKI Episodes and eGFR Trajectories Modify RAS Inhibitor Cardio‑Renal Risk in CKD: A Target Trial Emulation

detail.title: Dynamic AKI Episodes and eGFR Trajectories Modify RAS Inhibitor Cardio‑Renal Risk in CKD: A Target Trial Emulation

detail.abstract:
Background: Whether acute kidney injury (AKI) episodes and subsequent eGFR trajectories modify the cardiorenal effects of renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a daily clinical dilemma with no direct evidence. Current guidelines recommend RAS inhibitors across all CKD stages, but the physiological effects of reducing intraglomerular pressure could be deleterious in kidneys with recent tubular injury and impaired autoregulation. We aimed to determine whether dynamic AKI history alters the association between RAS inhibitor use and the composite risk of cardiovascular events, end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), and rapid eGFR decline. 

Methods: We conducted a target trial emulation using electronic health records (2003–2020) from a tertiary hospital in China. Eligible participants were adults (≥18 years) with CKD stages 1–5, no prior RAS inhibitor use, and no contraindications. The intervention was RAS inhibitor initiation versus non-use. The primary outcome was a composite of cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, coronary revascularization, cerebral infarction, cerebral haemorrhage, or lacunar infarction), ESKD, ≥40% eGFR decline, or doubling of serum creatinine. We used inverse probability‑weighted marginal structural models (MSMs) with time‑varying covariates for AKI episodes, severity, and recovery status. E‑values were calculated to assess robustness to unmeasured confounding. 

Findings: Among 69,242 patients (mean age 58.2 years, 47.2% female), 11,284 (16.3%) experienced at least one AKI episode. RAS inhibitor use was more common in AKI patients (58.1% vs. 51.5%, p<0.001). Over a median follow‑up of 2.8 years, 5,361 patients (8.8%) experienced the composite outcome (22.1% in AKI vs. 6.2% in no AKI). In MSMs, RAS inhibitor effects were significantly modified by dynamic kidney function. Among patients without AKI, RAS inhibitors showed a neutral association (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.94–1.24). By contrast, patients with AKI experienced progressively increasing risk: single episode (HR 1.58, 95% CI 1.37–1.82), multiple episodes (HR 2.11, 95% CI 1.68–2.65; p for interaction <0.001). Incomplete AKI recovery conferred higher risk (HR 1.92, 95% CI 1.58–2.33) than complete recovery (HR 1.29, 95% CI 1.08–1.54). E‑values ranged from 1.48 to 2.98, indicating robustness to unmeasured confounding. Static metabolic phenotypes did not modify the effect (p for interaction >0.1 for all comparisons). 

Interpretation: Dynamic AKI episodes and post‑AKI eGFR trajectories are powerful modifiers of RAS inhibitor effects on cardiorenal outcomes in CKD. The increased risk is concentrated in patients with AKI history, especially those with multiple episodes or incomplete recovery. A patient's dynamic kidney history—rather than static metabolic phenotype—should guide the risk‑benefit assessment of RAS inhibitor therapy, challenging the current one‑size‑fits‑all guideline recommendation.

title: Does Inflation Targeting Matter in Achieving Long-term Price Stability? Evidence from Egypt and Georgia
affiliations: Central Bank of Lebanon, American University of Beirut and Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies (IHEID) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Does Inflation Targeting Matter in Achieving Long-term Price Stability? Evidence from Egypt and Georgia
detail.abstract: This study investigates the role of an inflation-targeting (IT) regime in shaping inflation persistence and mitigating potential spillovers from external shocks analogous to the COVID-19 pandemic. Egypt and Georgia provide a near-ideal comparative setting for assessing whether inflation-targeting credibility shapes inflation dynamics. Both countries carry food shares of approximately 30 percent in their consumer price index baskets and have structurally comparable import profiles, implying broadly equivalent exposure to commodity price shocks. Yet their inflation outcomes have diverged sharply: Georgia adopted IT in 2009, while Egypt has only recently adopted it. Employing Bayesian estimation of a Quarterly Projection Model, we show that Georgia’s IT framework, is associated with near-unity forward-looking weight in core inflation dynamics and negligible food-to-core spillovers, whereas Egypt exhibits strong backward-looking inertia and substantial pass-through from food shocks. A key policy implication is that the Georgian experience offers a credible roadmap for non-adopter or recent-adopter countries: when Georgia adopted IT, its fiscal fundamentals were not materially stronger than Egypt’s current position, suggesting that the regime choice itself, alongside complementary institutional reforms, can build the credibility needed to anchor expectations.

detail.abstract: Since employment dynamics are persistent, a central bank's dual mandate to promote maximum employment and price stability naturally generates history dependence in monetary policy. This history dependence under a dual mandate flattens the reducedform Phillips curve, reduces the volatility of inflation in response to demand shocks, and improves outcomes at the zero lower bound. Moreover, we show that a dual mandate can be observationally equivalent to average inflation targeting following a demand shock. However, this equivalence breaks down in the presence of supply shocks. We first illustrate these findings analytically and then examine their quantitative importance in a model with nominal rigidities and labor search frictions calibrated to match U.S. business-cycle moments. An employment mandate can naturally provide the stabilization benefits associated with history-dependent policy frameworks.

title: Reconsidering the 0·8 m/s Slow-Gait Threshold in African Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

detail.title: Reconsidering the 0·8 m/s Slow-Gait Threshold in African Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis

detail.abstract:
Background: Gait speed below 0·8 m/s underpins international screening for sarcopenia and the Motoric Cognitive Risk syndrome, but the threshold was derived from high-income cohorts. No continent-wide pooled estimate of mean gait speed, slow-gait prevalence, or determinants has been published for African older adults.

Methods: Six databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, OpenAlex, CINAHL Complete, Semantic Scholar, WHO IRIS) were searched for peer-reviewed observational studies reporting gait speed in community-dwelling adults with a cohort mean or median age of 50 years or older in any African country. Two reviewers screened and extracted independently. Risk of bias was appraised with the Joanna Briggs Institute Prevalence Checklist. Pooled estimates used random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood, Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals, and 95% prediction intervals. PROSPERO CRD420261387756.

Findings: Of 2,884 records, 26 studies were included and 10 contributed to quantitative synthesis. Pooled mean gait speed across the primary pool (eight studies, N=16,561) was 0·83 m/s (95% CI 0·68 to 0·98; prediction interval 0·39 to 1·27). Pooled slow-gait prevalence across four studies (N=4,881) was 43·6% (95% CI 9·2 to 82·0%; prediction interval 0 to 100%). Walking protocol was the largest moderator (static-start 0·79 m/s vs dynamic-start 1·08 m/s; Q=22·9, p<0·0001). Older age, female sex, lower education, and stroke or ischaemic heart disease were consistent determinants of slower gait.

Interpretation: The pooled African mean sits at the 0·8 m/s clinical threshold, so applying that cut-off classifies about half of community-dwelling older adults as impaired. Existing international mobility thresholds may require validation before application in African ageing populations.

detail.abstract:
The dollar’s share of global official foreign exchange reserves fell from 64 percent in 2015 to 56 percent in 2025. This downward trajectory is sometimes read as evidence that the dollar’s role in international financial markets is eroding. However, aggregate statistics obscure the composition of changes occurring at the country level. In this post, we show that the aggregate decline is not a systematic global shift away from dollar assets. Rather, the aggregate decline reflects the actions of a handful of large reserve holders, changing either their currency preferences or the size of their reserve portfolio. From the perspective of the cross section of countries holding dollar assets, the dollar’s status in official portfolios is largely intact.

detail.abstract:
Background: Gait speed below 0·8 m/s underpins international screening for sarcopenia and the Motoric Cognitive Risk syndrome, but the threshold was derived from high-income cohorts. No continent-wide pooled estimate of mean gait speed, slow-gait prevalence, or determinants has been published for African older adults.

Methods: Six databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, OpenAlex, CINAHL Complete, Semantic Scholar, WHO IRIS) were searched for peer-reviewed observational studies reporting gait speed in community-dwelling adults with a cohort mean or median age of 50 years or older in any African country. Two reviewers screened and extracted independently. Risk of bias was appraised with the Joanna Briggs Institute Prevalence Checklist. Pooled estimates used random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood, Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals, and 95% prediction intervals. PROSPERO CRD420261387756.

Findings: Of 2,884 records, 26 studies were included and 10 contributed to quantitative synthesis. Pooled mean gait speed across the primary pool (eight studies, N=16,561) was 0·83 m/s (95% CI 0·68 to 0·98; prediction interval 0·39 to 1·27). Pooled slow-gait prevalence across four studies (N=4,881) was 43·6% (95% CI 9·2 to 82·0%; prediction interval 0 to 100%). Walking protocol was the largest moderator (static-start 0·79 m/s vs dynamic-start 1·08 m/s; Q=22·9, p<0·0001). Older age, female sex, lower education, and stroke or ischaemic heart disease were consistent determinants of slower gait.

Interpretation: The pooled African mean sits at the 0·8 m/s clinical threshold, so applying that cut-off classifies about half of community-dwelling older adults as impaired. Existing international mobility thresholds may require validation before application in African ageing populations.

detail.abstract: Under stated valuation assumptions, a share price can express how long earning power must persist. It cannot explain why that persistence is credible. detail.abstract: Environmental, regulatory, and economic exogenous disruptions force companies within the maritime shipping industry to become more sustainable. Financing for implementing the necessary changes is particularly challenging for these companies, considering their narrow margins. With the changes in the shipping industry being intrinsically capital-intensive, funding is a particular issue, as few institutional or individual investors can provide the capital required. This paper investigates the challenges of financing. Drawing from the theory of pecking order on debt and equity, it conceptualizes the relation between the modes of financing for the maritime shipping companies and the nature of the disruptions. Initially, we analyze the various IMO decarbonization regulations, GHG emissions, alternative fuels, and green energy. Moreover, the relationship between fleet operation and management and finance is explored. The paper provides a framework to illustrate from a financial perspective the plethora of challenges and disruptions that have troubled the industry. We then recommend more suitable funding routes for companies to gauge the proper mix of equity and debt levels, bonds, and leverage, based on the company's characteristics, such as size or ESG performance, as analyzed via the lens of corporate financing, along with the nature of the disruption, such as high inflation or geopolitical conflicts. In more detail, the paper focuses on key environmental, social, and governance (ESG) drivers both in the short-term and the long-term within the dry bulk shipping industry: impact investing and ESG factors are driving new investment opportunities and contributing to risk mitigation and long-term investment returns. The most pressing financial and economic questions of the time are wildly extended equity and bond valuations, inflation, and the conundrum most central banks face. Given these uncertainties, from an investment perspective for equity markets, the risk/return outlook for risk assets is skewed to the downside, making a cautious approach prudent for maritime shipping companies.

detail.abstract: Securities lending-the temporary transfer of securities in exchange for collateral-is essential to the modern financial system, facilitating short selling, market making, and efficient liquidity management. Yet, little is known about how these contracts are priced. Using comprehensive transaction-level data, we identify the determinants of returns from lending the same security against cash or securities collateral. We develop a model in which lending returns compensate for security risk, illiquidity, and the use of scarce dealer balance-sheet capacity. We also define a return wedge between the two market segments. Consistent with the model, the wedge widens with risk, illiquidity, dealer constraints, and collateral reusability but narrows as participation across both segments increases.

detail.abstract: India is the world's largest mobile user base for ChatGPT and the third-largest for DeepSeek, yet contributes between 0.1 and 1% of accepted papers at top artificial intelligence (AI) conferences and has produced no frontier-class AI architectures or foundation models. The Stanford AI Index records India at roughly 8-9% of global AI publications, yet India remains largely absent from the rankings of notable models and high-impact AI research.India's Rs.10,372 Cr IndiaAI Mission allocates nothing to fundamental AI research in theory, algorithms, or mathematical foundations. This paper argues that AI sovereignty-the capacity to build, deploy, and govern indigenous AI capabilities-cannot be achieved through an application-and-services strategy alone. Drawing on bibliometric evidence from the Stanford AI Index, Scopus, and the IndiaML tracker, as well as comparative analysis of China's trajectory from AI follower to near-parity with the United States, we show that foundational research capability is the binding constraint on India's AI self-reliance story. To remedy this situation, we propose a set of policy interventions: earmarking a dedicated AI research fund within the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), reforming UGC and AICTE promotion criteria from publication count to research quality, and creating a small number of autonomous, privately funded or public-private frontier research labs focused on high-risk, long-horizon AI research. We further argue that India should build capability not only in current foundation-model technologies, but also in two or three plausible next-generation directions where a future technological disruption may create new opportunities for leadership. Together, these measures can expand India's frontier research capacity while reducing the risk of remaining permanently in catch-up mode.

detail.abstract: Coalition loyalty programs (CLPs) enable consumers to earn and redeem rewards across multiple firms, influencing search behavior and competition. This paper develops a theoretical model where CLPs endogenously create firm prominence by altering consumers' search order. We show that CLP firms raise prices due to cost pass-through and increased willingness to pay, while consumers may still benefit from rewards. We derive conditions under which a single CLP is both profitable and beneficial to consumers and note that this may occur even when the reward is small and does not create any intrinsic value. We characterize the organizer's optimal program design, including the reward offered to consumers, using a set of contractual instruments that allow us to fully endogenize participation, pricing, and coalition formation. We show that CLP competition reduces prices and enhances consumer surplus when non-CLP firms remain, but when only CLPs compete, higher prices and reduced search may harm consumers. Taken together, the results show that CLPs materially influence market dynamics, firm profitability, and welfare.

detail.abstract: This Report summarises the proceedings of a workshop on Combatting Corruption and Collusion in Public Procurement, which considered mechanisms for better protecting public procurement processes from corruption and collusion. The authors, working in cooperation with the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), hosted the one-day workshop at King’s College London. The workshop brought together experts from UK Government ministerial departments engaged in public procurement activities, the CMA, the  Serious Fraud Office (SFO), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the Canadian Competition Bureau, the Comisión Nacional de los Mercados y la Competencia (the Spanish competition authority), and the Norwegian Klagenemndssekretariatet (Appeals Board Secretariat), along with academic and practising lawyers and economists. Workshop participants discussed a range of measures that could be considered to ensure a more proactive, integrated, and coordinated approach to fighting corruption and collusion in public procurement, and the creation of a more resilient, and pro-competitive, public procurement system. Discussions centred not only on the question of how to deter collusion and corruption through ex post law enforcement, but also on how better to prevent this conduct from happening in the first place (how to reduce both opportunities and incentives for this conduct to occur during public procurement processes). It was also considered how governments can ensure that overpayments made as a result of corruption or collusion during public procurement processes are recovered. A theme permeating the workshop sessions was how deeper coordination between agencies and institutions can be developed to better achieve these objectives. In summarising the proceedings, the Report seeks to shine a spotlight on the enduring nature of related problems, to propose potential solutions to them, and to highlight the importance of continuing dialogue in this area.

detail.abstract: Research in macroeconomics finds that aggregate economic uncertainty from real activities (e.g., employment, manufacturing, consumer spending) lags business cycle shifts while aggregate economic uncertainty from financial activities (e.g., dividend and price growth rates, bond yields) precedes such shifts. Such timing differences indicate that these sources of aggregate economic uncertainty vary in their predictability. Economic theory posits that such differential predictability will affect whether and how firms will shield managerial pay from uncontrollable uncertainty. Motivated by theory, we hypothesize and find that, consistent with a differential effect, CEO compensation decreases with macroeconomic uncertainty, but does not change with financial uncertainty. We also find that compensation structure diverges between the types of uncertainty, with a smaller (larger) proportion of incentive pay for macroeconomic (financial) uncertainty. As one would naturally expect, the nature of these relations varies as a function of a firm's sensitivity to aggregate uncertainty (i.e., a firm's uncertainty beta). Additional analyses provide evidence indicating that the differences in compensation we document reflect differences in the controllability of uncertainty and firms' sensitivity to that uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay is a major driver of resource utilisation, hospital costs, and critical care capacity strain, particularly among patients with severe cardiovascular conditions. Anticipating prolonged ICU stay early in the admission trajectory remains challenging, limiting opportunities for proactive resource planning. This study develops and evaluates a medication-aware multimodal machine learning framework for early prediction of prolonged ICU length of stay using only information available within the first 24 hours of ICU admission. Using the MIMIC-IV database, a cardiovascular critical care cohort including patients with acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, cardiogenic shock, and cardiac arrest was constructed. Predictors incorporated first-day physiological measurements, laboratory results, respiratory support indicators, medication exposures capturing early therapeutic intensity and treatment context, demographic and administrative characteristics under leakage-safe temporal constraints. Multiple machine learning models were evaluated using a precision-constrained recall optimisation strategy aligned with operational planning objectives. Among evaluated models, including logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and a random forest–XGBoost ensemble, CatBoost achieved the strongest overall performance, attaining an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.82 and an area under the precision–recall curve (PR-AUC) of 0.65 on the held-out test set while maintaining a minimum precision of 0.60. Medication exposure variables provided meaningful incremental predictive value beyond physiological and laboratory measurements, with removal of medication features reducing recall despite stable discrimination. These findings demonstrate that medication-aware multimodal modelling of early ICU data can support temporally valid prediction of prolonged ICU stay and proactive resource planning.

affiliations: Harvard Kennedy School, Tilburg University and Cornell University

detail.title: Tracking Inequality: Teachers and the Allocation of Educational Opportunities
detail.abstract:
Professionals routinely make consequential decisions for others without systematically observing how those decisions turn out. Whether such decisions reflect accurate forecasting or systematically distorted beliefs has important implications for equality of opportunity. We study this question in the context of teachers' recommendations for high school tracks by combining nationwide administrative data, randomized vignette experiments, belief elicitation, and a field experiment. Holding students' academic performance and interests constant, teachers are significantly less likely to recommend demanding academic tracks when students come from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds. This differential treatment is accompanied by systematically inaccurate beliefs: teachers substantially overestimate the probability that high-achieving disadvantaged students will fail in academically demanding schools. We then provide teachers with personalized feedback on their previous recommendations and objective information on the realized success of disadvantaged students. The intervention substantially reduces socioeconomic gaps in recommendations for high-achieving students. Effects are concentrated among boys assigned to teachers with the largest prior recommendation gaps and the most inaccurate beliefs. Among the high-achieving disadvantaged boys most affected by the intervention, these changes translate into higher enrollment in demanding academic tracks, without detectable adverse effects on short-run academic performance.

title: Rational Inattention to Discrete Choices with Stable Priors

detail.title: Rational Inattention to Discrete Choices with Stable Priors
detail.abstract:
How does prior information affect discrete choice? In the seminal rational inattention model of Matějka and McKay (2015), multinomial logit arises from the discrete choice of agents who are uncertain about choice payoffs and who have access to a flexible information acquisition technology (RI-logit). A key limitation of this powerful framework is the lack of known solutions that allow the decision maker's prior information to vary across choices: obtaining such solutions has remained an open problem in this literature. In this paper, I solve the RI-logit model analytically for two related families of priors known respectively as Positive Stable and Tempered Stable distributions. In my solution, the decision maker's prior information enters the choice probabilities through a choice-specific parameter, which can be read as shifting either the ex-ante expected utility of a risk-neutral decision maker, or the ex-ante riskiness perceived by a risk-averse one. These results complete the RI-logit framework by separating prior information from information that is endogenously acquired, and expand its empirical applications by making it possible to study how choice probabilities react to changes in prior information.

detail.abstract: Today, medical devices from heart rhythm monitors and hospital infusion pumps to implantable devices can connect to increasingly broad portions of the hospital network, much more than just the perimeter, creating an enlarged attack surface for healthcare delivery organizations. Distributed ledger technology has been touted as a way to maintain the integrity and provenance of the telemetry these devices transmit, but the cryptographic primitives almost all current blockchains build on elliptic-curve signatures and RSA-based key exchange-are demonstrably broken if there is practical large-scale quantum computers using Shor's algorithm. A secure ledger today but one that is outdated should be broken within a patient's lifespan, that doesn't ensure their data would stay reliable over the next few decades. This paper compiles relevant latest articles on PQC, PUF and permissioned blockchain designs to suggest a five-layer framework, which provides potential solutions for quantum-resistant CDD sharing in connected medical devices. It's architecture includes key encapsulation mechanisms and signatures standardized by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) which are based on lattices combined with a hardware-based device identity and proof of integrity using Merkle. The diversity of sources spanning 45 peer-reviewed and standards body papers with the majority published from 2019 to 2025 were studied to characterize the state of the art, explore common quantum resistant primitive design patterns, and to quantify the computational overhead that quantum-resistant primitives carry for resource-constrained devices. The review identifies three possible paths for migration: hybrid classical-plus-post-quantum handshakes, lightweight authenticated encryption at the edge, and hash-based long-term signatures-which have yet to be resolved-along with initial progress in key-size inflation and in achieving regulatory alignment. The proposed architecture and the respective evaluation criteria are for guidance for other empirical implementation and standardisation in the area of the digital health infrastructure.

detail.abstract:
We study the effects of vast increases in U.S. small business program eligibility standards, which expanded larger firms' access to support for small businesses. Exploiting quasi-random variation in the timing of these expansions and using administrative Census data, we show that revenues decline for the smallest firms, particularly those that are younger, more productive, and financially constrained. Government procurement contracts also are reallocated to larger firms. Consequently, firm exits increase, wages decline, and patenting falls. These findings highlight the economic consequences of expanding eligibility: by crowding out the smallest firms, resources shift away from high-potential firms, reducing dynamism and innovation.

detail.abstract:
Why do we have so many meetings? Few workplace features are so scorned, yet seemingly so necessary. This paper provides the first large-scale economic evidence on workplace meetings using an original survey of more than 9,000 workers linked to matched employer–employee administrative data from Norway. We show that meetings are both common and costly, consuming an average of 12 percent of work hours and 14 percent of firm wage bills. Planning, problem solving, information sharing, and project coordination account for the majority of meeting activity. High-paying and high-revenue firms devote more resources to meetings despite facing a substantially higher opportunity cost of employee time. Meeting frequency and intensity are positively related to worker wage growth. Workers in meeting-intensive firms report greater on-the-job learning, and interactions with more senior colleagues are associated with stronger wage growth, suggesting that knowledge transmission within firms is an important mechanism. Meetings are the broccoli of work – widely disliked, but probably good for us anyway.

title: Unemployment Insurance in Macroeconomic Stabilization with Imperfect Expectations

detail.title: Unemployment Insurance in Macroeconomic Stabilization with Imperfect Expectations
detail.abstract:
Automatic stabilizers can respond to a recession without a new policy decision, but their effects on aggregate demand may still only arrive with delay. We study the transmission lag for unemployment insurance extensions in a heterogeneous-agent New Keynesian model that closely matches the incidence of unemployment risk and the response of household spending to job loss and UI extensions. More generous UI stimulates demand largely by relaxing precautionary saving, so households must anticipate future unemployment risk and benefit duration. To quantify this channel, we work directly with survey expectations, using a measured history of forecast errors and revisions, rather than committing to a specific model of belief formation. Our estimated model implies a significant Expectations-Driven Efficacy Lag. The direct effect of UI extensions on consumption peaks only after UI duration has begun to recede. In general equilibrium, the consumption multiplier is about 0.6 on impact, about half its value under full-information rational expectations, but the policy becomes more effective by the end of the first year of the recession.

detail.title: The Allocative Cost of War: A View to a Kill...ing of Productivity
detail.abstract:
Why is war so economically costly? Our answer is that modern war lowers output not only by destroying productive factors, but also by making the surviving economy work less efficiently. Using uniquely comprehensive firm-level data collected during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, we document a dramatic collapse in allocative productivity in Ukraine. To sharpen identification and explore key mechanisms (including the role of war intensity, internal displacement, reallocation, and macroeconomic instability), we exploit spatial heterogeneity across Ukrainian districts and comparisons with Russian aggression in 2014 and the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. Our key policy implication is that restoring allocative efficiency–and preparing institutional arrangements that facilitate rapid reallocation in times of stress–is critical for sustaining economic capacity, defense, and national security.

title: “Non-Marginal” Investor Beliefs

detail.title: “Non-Marginal” Investor Beliefs
detail.abstract:
This paper provides evidence of how the beliefs of investors who step out of the market, or “non-marginal” investors, influence asset prices. Using more than two decades of respondent-level investor surveys, we construct wedge measures that quantify the distance between subjective investor beliefs and option-implied benchmarks. We use self-identified proxies for market participation to document that these wedges correspond with the beliefs of non-marginal investors. Non-marginal investors are generally more pessimistic in their market return forecasts and perceive greater crash risks than the pricing population. Subjective crash beliefs are a key determinant of participation, even when controlling for expected return beliefs. This heterogeneity, in part, explains the negative association between average expected returns estimated from surveys and future realized market returns. In the cross-section, stocks with greater sensitivity to non-marginal beliefs earn lower returns, particularly where disagreement is high. Taken together, the results provide evidence of a composition channel in which belief-driven exit concentrates risk among fewer investors.

Discrimination operates in both directions: older applicants are disadvantaged in entry-level jobs, while younger applicants are less likely to be hired into managerial roles. A model of statistical discrimination with imperfect signal screening explains these patterns. Consistent with the model, older applicants to entry-level jobs are negatively selected relative to their peers.

detail.title: Air Pollution and Learning
detail.abstract:
Nearly the entire world's population breathes air exceeding WHO pollution guidelines, but the extent to which that exposure impairs the accumulation of human capital is not well understood. We study this using longitudinal PSAT data on nearly 10 million U.S. high school students, comparing the same student's scores across attempts preceded by differing air quality and instrumenting for local PM2.5 with smoke from distant wildfires. A year of observed pollution exposure reduces learning by 0.04-0.06 standard deviations, or 14-19% of typical annual score growth. The damage comes almost entirely from moderate pollution days (8–12 μg/m3), below the EPA's historical standard, and from exposure during the school year rather than summer, pointing to instructional disruption as a mechanism. Effects are three times larger in disadvantaged schools and among Black and Hispanic students, who are harmed more by the same exposure. Exposure to air pollution widens achievement gaps.

title: The Limits of Verifiability: Credibility and Flexibility in Communication

detail.title: The Limits of Verifiability: Credibility and Flexibility in Communication
detail.abstract:
We compare verifiable and unverifiable communication in a sender–receiver setting with partially aligned preferences, where the sender knows more than what her evidence can prove. We identify a credibility–flexibility tradeoff: tying the sender’s claims to her evidence enhances her credibility, but limits how flexibly she can communicate when her evidence does not accurately reflect her private information. This tradeoff changes the economics of verifiable disclosure. When preferences are sufficiently aligned, full evidence disclosure is neither sustainable in equilibrium nor efficient. We show that verifiability facilitates communication when preferences are sufficiently misaligned, but hinders it when they are sufficiently aligned, suggesting that institutions that impose verification need not al- ways improve information transmission. Finally, we study how verifiable and unverifiable communication can complement one another when both are available: unverifiable communication can contextualize verifiable evidence when the latter is misleading.

detail.title: Dynamic Investment and Product Market Rivalry: the Network Q Model
detail.abstract:
We present a new dynamic model of corporate investment in imperfectly competitive product markets that extends the neoclassical (Q) theory of capital to accommodate heterogeneous, multi-product firms and a rich hedonic demand system. Our model endogenizes firms' markups and generalizes Tobin's Q to a matrix (or network) of product market spillovers, which captures how each firm's investment affects that of its rivals. We provide equilibrium existence and uniqueness results along with global analytical solutions for the firms' investment policies. We then take our model to the data for the universe of US public companies and obtain four novel insights: 1) product market competition is a key driver of aggregate investment and capital allocation; 2) shocks to firms' cost of capital generate highly heterogeneous investment and markup responses across firms, and thus impact industry concentration; 3) monopoly rents account for a large, rising share of firms' value; 4) mergers consummated since 1995 have led to a modest decline in the aggregate capital formation of merging firms, yet firm-level markup increases have been highly heterogeneous.

detail.title: Rust in Motion: The Political Environmental Trap of Vehicle Tax Exemptions
detail.abstract:
Transportation is a major source of greenhouse gas and air pollution emissions worldwide, with most automobile pollution coming from vehicles older than 10 years. Yet, many policies discourage the removal of older vehicles from the fleet, with potential consequences for pollution and public health. This paper examines an equity-motivated anti-scrappage policy in Brazil using a border-pair design that exploits state variation in the age thresholds for vehicle ownership tax exemptions. Using municipality-level vehicle registration data from 2013-2020, we find that lower exemption age thresholds increase the average fleet age by up to one year, as they encourage owners to retain vehicles until they qualify for tax exemptions. Using fleet- and satellite-based estimates of pollution and administrative health data, we show that these policies increase on-road CO2 emissions per capita by up to 23% and PM2.5 concentrations by 4%, while deteriorating infant health outcomes. Leveraging state reforms that raised exemption ages, we find evidence that incumbents face greater electoral penalties wherever a greater share of the vehicle fleet re-enters the tax base, consistent with a “political environmental trap.” Within an MVPF framework, we find that lowering the exemption age by five years generates a net welfare loss of $0.78 for every $1 of forgone government revenue.

detail.title: The Impact of Patient Capital
detail.abstract:
We show that investor patience shapes venture-capital (VC) investment strategies and outcomes. Through a randomized experiment with Chinese fund managers, we demonstrate that managers explicitly tailor fund duration and project holding periods to the perceived horizons of their limited partner (LP) base. We find consistent evidence in the field, exploiting a 2014 Chinese reform that opened RMB-denominated VC funds to insurers. We compare treated RMB funds to unaffected USD-denominated funds run by the same general partners (GPs), both investing in Chinese startups. Insurer entry reshaped the LP base by displacing shorter-horizon investors such as individuals. Consequently, treated funds shifted strategy toward longer holding periods and earlier-stage investments, leading to improved portfolio company exits and innovation. Our results highlight the importance of patient ultimate investors in building a successful VC ecosystem, and offer a cautionary note on the ongoing retailization of private markets.

detail.title: Expectations-based Capital Inflow Shocks
detail.abstract:
Identifying the impact of capital inflows on output is challenging because inflows are forward-looking and respond to expectations about future economic conditions. We develop a new measure of capital inflow shocks using a simple and broadly applicable expectations-based framework that isolates the unexpected component of inflows by purging movements predicted by professional forecasters’ expectations. Estimates using the new measure for 27 emerging market economies indicate that capital inflows have sizable expansionary effects on output, operating through stronger domestic consumption and investment and easier financing conditions. Additional analysis indicates that equity-type inflows generate greater and more persistent effects than debt-type inflows, while large inflow reversals result in more pronounced effects than comparable increases in inflows. These results are robust to a wide range of alternative specifications.

title: Fiscal Policy and the Saving Glut of the Rich

detail.title: Fiscal Policy and the Saving Glut of the Rich
detail.abstract:
Since the 1980s, the United States has experienced a pronounced saving glut of the rich, a large accumulation of assets among the top 1% of earners. We argue that this development partly reflects a shift in the financing of redistributive policies, from inflationary finance in the 1960s and 1970s to debt finance backed by future taxation beginning in the early 1980s. The central insight is that, in the presence of a progressive tax system, a switch from inflationary to debt financing leads to debt accumulation by top earners. We develop a New Keynesian model with borrowers and savers in which redistributive transfers can be either funded or unfunded. Unfunded transfers generate fiscal inflation that erodes the real value of public and private debt, redistributing wealth through asset revaluation effects. Funded transfers, by contrast, are financed through future taxes borne primarily by high-income households, which respond by accumulating claims on both households and the government. Using a structurally estimated version of the model, we find that the shift from unfunded to funded redistribution in the 1980s contributed significantly to the subsequent saving glut of the rich.

detail.title: The No Surprises Act’s Surprises: Arbitration, Provider Network, and Insurer Pricing
detail.abstract:
The No Surprises Act (NSA) capped patients' liability for surprise bills and established federal final-offer arbitration for insurer–provider payment disputes. Linking arbitration records to the national longitudinal provider-insurer network panel and plan design data in the ACA marketplace, we find that the NSA reduced provider network participation in the specialties and states most affected by the reform, contrary to the standard prediction that removing balance billing makes network participation more attractive. The decline is consistent with arbitration strengthening providers' outside option: arbitration is high-volume and provider-favorable, with awards well above the statutory benchmark; and network participation declines after provider groups' first favorable arbitration outcomes. Suggestive evidence indicates that insurers more exposed to arbitration raise premiums. These results reveal an unintended consequence of the NSA: the law's direct consumer protections may be accompanied by narrower networks and higher premiums.

title: Behavioral Signatures of Cognitive Noise
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and Columbia University, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Department of Economics

detail.title: Behavioral Signatures of Cognitive Noise
detail.abstract:
The cognitive noise hypothesis is an increasingly popular explanation for a wide range of puzzling regularities in human behavior. Using simple, familiar tools and minimal assumptions drawn from neuroscience, cognitive noise models provide a parsimonious, unified explanation for a number of the most important anomalies documented in behavioral economics. The hypothesis proposes that limited cognitive resources force the brain to represent information imprecisely, generating coarser decisions, stochastic behavior and subjective uncertainty. Because brains deal with this kind of imprecision in a broadly Bayesian manner, imprecision leads to a number of well-known behavioral biases that may in fact be optimal given that imprecision. Because brains also allocate scarce cognitive resources adaptively, these biases and their severity are impacted by seemingly-irrelevant aspects of the choice environment, providing an explanation for a number of well-known context and experience effects that are otherwise difficult to explain. We review the basic structure of these models, their behavioral consequences, and the growing body of empirical evidence supporting them.

detail.title: Does AI Assistance Enhance or Erode Expertise? Evidence from a Three-Month Field Experiment in Patent Drafting
detail.abstract:
Whether AI assistance builds or erodes professional expertise is unsettled. In a pre-registered three-month randomized controlled trial, we gave 133 practicing patent lawyers at eleven U.S. intellectual property law firms access to a custom AI drafting assistant and measured both their performance while using AI and their professional judgment afterward without it. All work was scored by blinded expert patent attorneys. Paralleling findings from other white-collar domains, AI access raised the quality of work delivered on benchmark patent drafting tasks at 10 days (0.34 SD, p = 0.03) and 90 days (0.38 SD, p = 0.01), with larger gains among junior lawyers. After three months, all subjects redlined an existing patent application without AI, a core task of patent practice requiring expert judgment. Treated lawyers outperformed controls by 0.32 SD (p = 0.04), but this advantage was concentrated entirely among senior lawyers (0.45 SD, p = 0.02). Junior lawyers showed no average gain; their scores instead bifurcated, with sharply fewer mediocre scores offset by more poor and more good ones. The largest gains from AI thus accrued to the lawyers who retained the least. Foundational expertise may be a prerequisite for extracting durable skill from AI-assisted practice.

detail.title: Politics-driven Market Access and Its Cost: Evidence from China’s Grand Canal
detail.abstract:
Transportation networks often radiate from national capitals, reflecting political priorities as much as economic logic. How costly is infrastructure built for politics rather than markets? We study China’s Grand Canal: when the Mongols moved the capital from the central plain to Beijing, the canal followed, bypassing the economic core it once served. Using a grid-year panel spanning five dynasties (8th–19th centuries), we show the route best suited to reach the capital predicts the canal’s actual path. This redesign reshaped market access and, through it, population. Counterfactual analysis shows the canal raised population by 2.5–6.1%, but its politically motivated redesign cost 1.1–2.2%.

title: Will New Transportation Technologies Increase Urban Density

detail.title: Will New Transportation Technologies Increase Urban Density
detail.abstract:
Will 21st century transportation innovations work against urban density, as the car did in the 20th century, or promote urban centralization, as the railroad did in the 19th century? Reducing the cost of commuting always reduces urban centralization in the classic Alonso-Muth-Mills model but that result reverses if the number of trips is endogenous and the elasticity of trips with respect to their costs is greater than one. That elasticity may have increased over time, as an increasing share of daily trips seems to be discretionary and city centers increasingly provide entertainment. This paper asks discusses the urbanizing effects of four trends in transportation technology: shared mobility (such as Uber), autonomy (such as Waymo), vertical travel and green mobility, as provided by bike lane. As people spend more time travelling in denser, large areas, innovations that reduce the time cost of travel, such as autonomous cars, seem likely to complement urban living, as long as they don’t excessively increase traffic. Sharing is also easier in big cities, so technologies that involve sharing are also centripetal. The other trends seem less likely to have major effects. Moreover, the forces of inertia, which include both regulation and legacy infrastructure, are likely to limit the impact of any new technologies in Europe and the U.S., so that the biggest changes in urban form are likely to appear in east Asia and the developing world.

detail.title: The Multigenerational Effects of Legal Access to the Pill on Infant Health
detail.abstract:
We examine whether expanded legal access to the contraceptive pill for minors generated health benefits for subsequent generations. We use data from the restricted-use Natality files from 1970-2020, linking mothers to the level of access to the pill in their state and year of birth and the extent to which their mothers could access the pill as minors. Our results show that children whose mothers were born after expanded access to the pill as minors had better birth outcomes, with gains concentrated among Black families. Among affected births, legalization increased birth weight by 12-16 grams and reduced incidence of low birth weight by 2.7-3.4 percent. These magnitudes have economic significance, corresponding to approximately $113.8–$115.3 million in medical cost savings, measured in 2025 dollars, for the 2000 Black birth cohort alone. Our mechanism analysis points to a postponement of early childbearing by the generation directly affected by legal access to the pill as minors whose daughters subsequently attained higher levels of education, used more prenatal care, and had longer birth spacing. Taken together, our results suggest that reproductive health policy can generate multigenerational benefits and contribute to reductions in racial disparities in early-life health.

detail.title: An Empirically-Grounded Theory of Voting Based on Prosocial Motives
detail.abstract:
We propose a model of costly voting in a canonical spatial setting that reconciles key empirical features of electoral turnout. We integrate citizens with prosocial voting motives who realize higher payoffs from voting when (i) they expect more fellow supporters to vote, (ii) such votes collectively matter more for winning probabilities, and (iii) they care more about which candidate wins. We establish existence of Nash equilibria satisfying an additional condition that ensures equilibria correspond to those in a finite setting with many voters. We derive how electoral primitives—e.g., voter ideology, voting costs, elite polarization, expected closeness—affect outcomes such as turnout, turnout rates, and winning margins. We relate the predictions to empirical findings both from existing studies and our original data work. With all three prosocial motive components, our model reconciles the empirical regularities qualitatively and quantitatively; while existing models fail on multiple dimensions.

detail.title: Risk Perceptions of E-Cigarettes and the Evaluation of EVALI Messaging
detail.abstract:
With the growth of sales of e-cigarettes and other alternative nicotine products, governments face the new challenge of crafting public health messages that provide information to consumers about these less risky but not risk-free products. Bayesian learning serves as the theoretical framework for our analysis of how smokers form their perceptions of the risks of e-cigarettes based on the risks of smoking. This paper consists of two parts. First, we conduct a cross-country descriptive analysis of government messaging and smokers’ perceptions of e-cigarette risks. We study a diverse group of eight countries: Australia, China, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, Sweden, the U.K. and the U.S. We find that public health messages range widely across the countries. In online cross-country surveys of adult smokers, on average perceptions of e-cigarette risks are associated with their perceptions of the risk of smoking and with their countries’ messaging. Notably, in all eight countries many smokers incorrectly believe that e-cigarettes are relatively more harmful than smoking and over-estimate the absolute risks of e-cigarettes. In the second part of our study, we report the results of online randomized experiments that compare the effects of different e-cigarette risk messaging about an outbreak of lung injuries (given the acronym EVALI). The U.K. public health message about the low risk of e-cigarettes relative to smoking reduced smokers’ incorrect risk perceptions, while the U.S. public health message increased incorrect risk perceptions.

detail.abstract: Enforcement officers can employ traffic stops as legal justification to investigate a more serious offense. Our paper explores policies to limit potentially discriminatory and excessive pretextual stops in a setting where the stop and the search margins are linked and selection is a key mechanism. This study evaluated integrated N and phosphorus (P) fertilization effects on sorghum productivity and fertilizer N-use efficiency (FNUE) using ¹⁵N isotope tracing in a sandy Entisol of North Lombok, Indonesia. A randomized block design with 16 N–P combinations and three replications was used. Nitrogen was applied as ¹⁵N-labelled urea at 0, 69, 138, and 207 kg N ha⁻¹, while P was applied as triple superphosphate at 0, 34.5, 69, and 138 kg P₂O₅ ha⁻¹. Nitrogen and P application and their interaction significantly affected nutrient uptake and biomass production (p < 0.0001). The highest N uptake (95.69 kg ha⁻¹) and P uptake (52.88 kg ha⁻¹) occurred with 207 kg N + 69 kg P₂O₅ ha⁻¹. Fertilizer-derived N contributed up to 68.35% of N in stover and 80.18% in grain. The highest FNUE occurred with 69 kg N + 138 kg P₂O₅ ha⁻¹, indicating improved fertilizer-N utilization under balanced nutrition. Grain weight correlated positively with N uptake (r = 0.82) and FNUE (r = 0.33). Balanced N–P management can improve fertilizer efficiency and sustainable sorghum production in tropical dryland Entisols.

detail.title: A Dual Layer Approach for LLM Hallucination Reduction
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain prone to hallucinations: fluent, confident, factually incorrect statements that pose serious risks in medicine, law, finance, and scientific communication. Existing mitigation strategies are single-phase: retrieval-augmented generation grounds inputs but cannot validate outputs, while post-generation verifiers catch errors reactively but cannot prevent speculative generation. This paper proposes a training-free, model-agnostic, four-layer architecture built around two core components: a Pre-Generation Control Layer (PGCL), which performs domain and risk classification, evidence retrieval, and risk-calibrated decoding constraints before generation; and a Post-Generation Verification Layer (PGVL), which decomposes model output into atomic claims and verifies each against a hierarchical Tree-RAG index using an Entropy-Aware Dynamic TruthScore that tightens its acceptance threshold in proportion to the base model's generation-time uncertainty. A Surgical Self-Correction Loop rewrites only the specific span that fails verification, avoiding full response regeneration. We present the system design, a closed-form mathematical model of the entropy-aware threshold, and pilot evaluations on 50 HotpotQA queries (297 audited atomic claims, mean TruthScore 0.634, 95% CI [0.579, 0.687]) and 25 TruthfulQA queries under retrieval-sparse conditions. A matched-triplet ablation on 30 HotpotQA queries shows the entropy-aware dynamic threshold yields higher claim acceptance and mean TruthScore than a static threshold (0.631 vs. 0.397). On TruthfulQA, PGVL trades a modest reduction in confidently-wrong outputs (5/25 vs. 6/25) against lower raw accuracy, driven by correct answers converted to safe abstention -- a precision/recall trade-off we report transparently.

title: Bayesian Reconstruction of Ternary phase Diagrams from Machine- learned Atomistic Simulations: Application to In–Au–Hg Amalgam Design

detail.title: Bayesian Reconstruction of Ternary phase Diagrams from Machine- learned Atomistic Simulations: Application to In–Au–Hg Amalgam Design
detail.abstract:
Phase diagrams provide predictive design maps for materials by describing phase stability under specified thermodynamic conditions. In this work, we present a first-principles-based Bayesian framework for constructing temperature–composition phase diagrams of ternary alloys. The approach combines molecular dynamics simulations with Moment Tensor Potentials whose energy scale is experimentally corrected using the measured melting temperature of pure indium, and Gaussian process regression to reconstruct phase-specific Gibbs free-energy surfaces as functions of temperature, composition, and system size. The reconstructed free energies are extrapolated to the thermodynamic limit and used to determine phase coexistence, with confidence intervals accounting for both molecular dynamics sampling uncertainty and uncertainty in the bulk-limit extrapolation. The reconstruction is performed without imposing a parameterized Gibbs-energy model. 

      The methodology is applied to the In-rich In–Au–Hg system, relevant to amalgam lamp applications, and to its In–Au and In–Hg binary subsystems. The calculated binary phase diagrams show good agreement with experiment, while the ternary results recover the corresponding binary limits, confirming the internal consistency of the framework. The ternary phase diagram reveals a stable solid region corresponding to coexistence between bct-In and the intermetallic compound In2Au. This region enables the targeted identification of amalgam compositions that remain solid up to 140–150 °C, well above the stability range of conventional In–Hg systems.

title: Signal-analysis-driven Analog Conditioning for Weak Transient Signal Detection in Rapeseed Cleaning Loss Monitoring
affiliations: Jiangsu University, Jiangsu University, Jiangsu University, Jiangsu University and Jiangsu University

detail.title: Signal-analysis-driven Analog Conditioning for Weak Transient Signal Detection in Rapeseed Cleaning Loss Monitoring
detail.abstract: In cleaning-loss monitoring during rapeseed combine harvesting, traditional experience-based circuit design struggles to achieve stable triggering because single-grain impact signals are weak and interference is complex. To address this problem, this study proposes a hardware design method for loss monitoring based on signal analysis and analog signal conditioning. By integrating the grain impact sensing mechanism, kinematic decomposition, and the impulse–charge conversion relationship, the study analyzes the differences between the target signal and interference signals in both the time and frequency domains. Furthermore, based on the ratio of the energy retention rate of the target signal to that of the interference signals, a signal separation margin metric is proposed to enhance target-signal identification capability for weak rapeseed grain impacts, and is then used as a quantitative basis for the coordinated design of filter cutoff frequency and order, operational-amplifier gain allocation, and the envelope time constant. A signal conditioning chain was then established, comprising piezoelectric sensing, active filtering, signal amplification and unidirectional rectification, envelope extraction, and hysteresis comparison. At the signal-chain level, signal-chain modeling, LTspice simulation, and experimental measurements at key PCB nodes were used to validate the rationality of the proposed design method and the effectiveness with which the signal conditioning chain fulfills its intended functions. At the system level, bench testing was further performed to verify the application performance of the system. The results showed that the designed circuit could effectively preserve rapeseed grain impact responses while suppressing interference, thereby enabling stable single-event triggering of grain impacts. The square-wave pulses generated by grain impacts had widths of no more than 5 ms, with an average width of 2.3 ms. The monitoring system achieved a bench-test accuracy of over 97.5% and was further validated for field applicability. This study proposes a quantitative parameter design method for optimizing the recognition of weak transient target signals, centered on signal separation margin, establishes an integrated research framework spanning mechanism analysis, signal separation, parameter design, and system validation, and on this basis completes the hardware design of a rapeseed cleaning-loss monitoring device, thereby providing a useful reference for the design of online weak transient signal sensing systems for agricultural equipment operating under complex conditions.

title: Engineering Scalable Private Cellular IoT Connectivity for Smart Cities: A 3,200-SIM APN, VRF, and Cloud Integration Case Study

detail.title: Engineering Scalable Private Cellular IoT Connectivity for Smart Cities: A 3,200-SIM APN, VRF, and Cloud Integration Case Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
