detail.abstract: Large-scale Smart City Internet of Things (IoT) deployments require more than cellular coverage. They also require scalable endpoint addressing, controlled routing, network isolation, cloud connectivity, and operational processes capable of provisioning and validating large device inventories. This paper presents an observational network-engineering case study of a production Smart City deployment with a project scope of 3,200 Machine-to-Machine (M2M) SIMs. The implemented architecture connected cellular IoT endpoints to a cloud-hosted Smart City platform through a dedicated Private Access Point Name (APN), a dedicated Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instance within the telecommunications operator's IP backbone, Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routing integration between the packetswitched core and IP backbone, and a cloud firewall. Public Internet access was not permitted for the M2M SIMs. A private /20 IPv4 pool was allocated to the project, with individual provisioned SIMs receiving static private /32 addresses. SIM-to-IP mappings were prepared through a spreadsheetassisted workflow using formulas and AutoFill before submission to the responsible provisioning team. Approximately 3,200 address allocations could be prepared in around ten minutes. End-to-end private IP reachability was subsequently verified using more than ten IoT endpoints. During provisioning, one duplicate-address incident was observed in which the same private IP address became associated with two M2M SIMs. Packet-core troubleshooting identified the duplicate assignment, after which one address was changed and reprovisioned. The case demonstrates that large-scale cellular IoT engineering involves two interdependent scalability dimensions: network-plane scalability and provisioning-plane scalability. Based on these observations, the paper proposes a provisioning model incorporating centralized IP address management (IPAM), automatic uniqueness and range validation, authoritative SIM-to-IP inventory, controlled provisioning integration, automated post-provisioning verification, and lifecycle auditing.

title: Health Insurance Underwriting and the Heterogeneous Effects of the Affordable Care Act
affiliations: Columbia University,  and

detail.title: Health Insurance Underwriting and the Heterogeneous Effects of the Affordable Care Act
detail.abstract:
The Affordable Care Act, the largest US welfare reform since 1965, banned health insurance underwriting and rejections based on pre-existing conditions and introduced large premium subsidies for low- to middle-income individuals. Yet how many people the ban made better off, and how its effects varied by health risk, remain unknown—because data on who was rejected before the reform have been lacking. Using a proprietary dataset of pre-ACA insurance applications and underwriting decisions, we document, model, and estimate the reform's heterogeneous effects by age, income, and health risk. We find its benefits were concentrated among low-income, high-risk, or over-50 individuals.

title: Pensions and Turbulence: Automatic Adjustment, Risk, and Fairness in Long-Term Pension Design
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Pensions and Turbulence: Automatic Adjustment, Risk, and Fairness in Long-Term Pension Design
detail.abstract:
Public pension systems are long-term social contracts operating under persistent economic, demographic, and political uncertainty. Periods of turbulence, marked by financial shocks, changes in longevity, and shifting labour markets, test the capacity of pension institutions to adapt while maintaining adequacy, equity, and legitimacy. Building on earlier joint work on pension economics and reform with Nicholas Barr, this chapter analyses the role of automatic and semi-automatic adjustment mechanisms in public pension design. Drawing on comparative experience from Sweden, Canada, and the United States, we examine mechanisms for maintaining financial balance, the incorporation of life expectancy into retirement age and benefit design, and the accumulation and drawdown phases of defined contribution pensions. We argue that well-designed automatic mechanisms can discipline political decision-making and improve resilience, but only if they are proportionate, transparent, and attentive to distributional and intergenerational consequences. In turbulent times, good pension design does not eliminate the need for political choice; rather, it structures that choice so that adjustment can occur without repeated crises.

title: Rain Follows the Forest: Land Use Policy, Climate Change, and Adaptation
affiliations: ENSAE Paris, University of California, Santa Barbara and Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS)

detail.title: Rain Follows the Forest: Land Use Policy, Climate Change, and Adaptation
detail.abstract:
Human actions can alter the climate via land use. We analyze the 1930s Great Plains Shelterbelt, a large-scale forestation program across the US Midwest. The program increased precipitation and decreased temperatures for decades. We measure these changes in downwind counties where no trees were planted, isolating the effects of climate from those of afforestation and enabling us to study adaptation. Improved growing conditions allowed farmers to expand corn acreage and adopt water-intensive practices. In a period of farm consolidation, this altered the structure of the agricultural sector, contributing to the survival of small farms but less farm machine usage. The findings demonstrate the endogeneity of climate to land use change and the long-term impacts of tree planting on agricultural development.

title: Is a Dollar a Dollar? How Transfer Design Shapes Household Spending
affiliations: , Georgetown University and Georgetown University

detail.title: Is a Dollar a Dollar? How Transfer Design Shapes Household Spending
detail.abstract:
Government transfers vary along two design dimensions that standard models predict should not matter: whether benefits are paid in cash or kind, and whether they arrive as one-time or recurring payments. We test how these design choices affect household spending using sharp changes in four pandemic-era transfers to low-income families with children: one-time food vouchers, monthly food benefits, one-time cash payments, and monthly cash payments. Linking variation in benefit timing and amount to high-frequency household scanner data, we estimate spending responses in a harmonized difference-in-differences and event-study framework.Households spend more out of in-kind benefits than out of cash transfers of similar value, and more out of recurring than one-time transfers in the short run. Our estimates produce the first internally comparable set of short-run food-store MPCs across transfer types, ranging from 0.18 (one-time) and 0.38 (monthly) for in-kind benefits, versus 0.06 (one-time) and 0.20 (monthly) for cash. The patterns are consistent with mental accounting, labeling, and forward-looking responses. More broadly, transfer design—not just generosity and targeting—is an important policy lever for social insurance and short-run demand stabilization.

title: Do Online Job Postings Capture Job Vacancies?
affiliations: Bureau of Labor Statistics, University of Rochester and University of Oslo, Department of Economics

detail.title: Do Online Job Postings Capture Job Vacancies?
detail.abstract:
We ask whether online job postings capture U.S. job vacancies, matching near-universal Burning Glass (BG) postings to the representative Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). BG converged toward JOLTS over 2007–2022, and its representativeness varies across establishment characteristics. We reweight BG to align postings with JOLTS openings along observables, and assess impacts on prior BG findings. Because large establishments account for most openings and are well represented, the level and cyclicality of skill demand survive our adjustment. But BG overstates labor market concentration (the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index) nearly threefold, because small and mid-sized establishments post less online.

title: PLRD: Partially Linear Regression Discontinuity Inference
affiliations: Stanford University, Stanford Graduate School of Business and Stanford University - Department of Statistics

detail.title: PLRD: Partially Linear Regression Discontinuity Inference
detail.abstract:
Regression discontinuity designs have become one of the most popular research designs in empirical economics. We argue, however, that the widely used approaches to building confidence intervals in regression discontinuity designs often exhibit suboptimal behavior in practice. We propose a new estimator, the partially linear regression discontinuity (PLRD) estimator that, in set of a simulation studies carefully calibrated to twelve high-profile applications of regression discontinuity designs, has substantially lower estimation error than available comparison methods. Throughout our experiments, the confidence intervals built using PLRD are both valid and short. We also provide large-sample guarantees for PLRD. Our simulation study serves as a general template for how new econometric methods can be credibly evaluated relative to the existing alternatives by constructing simulation designs that generate synthetic data indistinguishable from the original data using the Wasserstein generative adversarial network methodology.

title: Comparisons
affiliations: and Harvard University

detail.title: Comparisons
detail.abstract:
Economic decisions are often shaped by comparison points such as reference points, goals, expectations and peers. A long-standing puzzle is that decisions sometimes increase in these comparators (assimilation) and sometimes decrease in them (contrast). We develop a simple taxonomy that predicts the sign. The idea is that when absolute evaluations—translating a decision input into an output—are difficult, people use comparison points as information about how to navigate tradeoffs. This logic predicts that decisions decrease in input comparators—those tied to exogenous decision inputs (e.g., a typical hourly wage)—and increase in output comparators—those tied to endogenous decisions or outcomes (e.g., typical daily earnings). We test and confirm these predictions in experiments on labor supply, investment and belief updating, involving both social and expectations-based comparison points. We further show that comparison effects weaken both when decision uncertainty is experimentally reduced and when comparators are less informative, consistent with a mechanism of comparisons as information. Finally, a classification of the prior literature suggests that the input-vs.-output taxonomy organizes the sign of comparison effects across more than 100 experimental and field observational studies.

title: Loan Rates as Incentive Instruments
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Loan Rates as Incentive Instruments
detail.abstract:
Loan rates are usually viewed as prices that shape borrower incentives, but they can also serve another role in a principal-agent problem by determining how informative repayment is about unobservable effort inside the bank. I study how the two roles interact: because loan rates move repayment probabilities differently for different borrowers, the bank designs its wage contract and its loan rate menu jointly. I show that the cost-minimizing wage contract is non-monotone, including pay after default, and that the bank tilts loan rates toward levels that make rewarded outcomes most diagnostic of correct assignment. When failure pay is restricted, the bank instead re-prices some loans toward the rate at which repayment probabilities are most similar across borrowers and may ultimately take more risk to conserve on agency costs. I show that a capital requirement introduced to correct a leverage externality caps failure pay in this way and, under a countercyclical capital requirement, the economy can enter a permanent two-point cycle in which banks alternate between non-monotone contracts with less risk-taking and monotone contracts with more.

title: Robustness of Federated Credit Risk Systems against Adversarial Attacks using BayesShield

detail.title: Robustness of Federated Credit Risk Systems against Adversarial Attacks using BayesShield

detail.abstract: This research introduces BayesShield, a novel defense framework designed to fortify federated credit risk systems against both poisoning and evasion attacks while preserving predictive accuracy and providing principled uncertainty quantification. BayesShield operates on two intertwined levels. First, at the client level, it employs a Bayesian neural network (BNN) with a Laplace approximation for posterior inference over local model weights. Instead of transmitting single-point gradient estimates, each participating institution communicates a compact representation of its posterior—specifically, the mean and a low-rank covariance matrix. This Bayesian aggregation mechanism fundamentally alters the game for adversaries. A poisoning attack that shifts the mean of the local posterior is rendered less effective because the aggregation step weights contributions by their inverse covariance, effectively down-weighting high-uncertainty or inconsistent updates. Furthermore, BayesShield incorporates a novel anomaly detection module that monitors the divergence between incoming local posteriors and the current global posterior, using a robust distance metric akin to the Wasserstein distance under a Gaussian assumption. Clients whose updates are statistical outliers, exhibiting excessive shift or inflated variance without corresponding data evidence, are flagged and their contributions are either down-weighted or entirely excluded via a dynamic consensus threshold.

title: From Weekly Searches to Monthly Inflation: Feature Engineering and Machine Learning for Inflation Nowcasting in India
affiliations: Jamia Millia Islamia New Delhi and Jamia Millia Islamia

detail.title: From Weekly Searches to Monthly Inflation: Feature Engineering and Machine Learning for Inflation Nowcasting in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Can Google searches be useful for nowcasting inflation? This study examines whether highfrequency Google search activity can improve monthly inflation nowcasting in India and, more importantly, whether the way search information is represented affects forecasting performance. Using weekly Google Trends data for 166 keywords covering 10 thematic categories over January 2012-December 2025, we construct four alternative representations of search activity to address the frequency mismatch between weekly search data and monthly inflation. For this we considered monthly averages, within-month statistical features, lagged statistical features, and weekly-pivot features. These representations are evaluated using a range of machine-learning methods, including LASSO, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, Support Vector Regression, AdaBoost, K-Nearest Neighbours, Decision Tree, and Linear Regression. To assess the role of model complexity and mixed-frequency modelling, we further compare the machine-learning specifications with Beta-MIDAS and five deeplearning architectures, namely LSTM, ANN(BPNN), 1D-CNN, GRU, and Bi-LSTM. The results demonstrate that the representation of high-frequency search information is crucial for inflation nowcasting. Simple monthly averaging provides useful predictive information, but incorporating within-month statistical characteristics substantially improves forecasting performance. The largest improvement is obtained when these characteristics are combined with one-, two-, and three-month lags, with LASSO achieving the best performance among the proposed Google Trends specifications (RMSE = 0.73, MAE = 0.59, R² = 0.82). This specification also outperforms the conventional Random Walk, AR(1), and ARIMA benchmarks in terms of RMSE. In contrast, Beta-MIDAS and the deep-learning models do not outperform the best regularized machine-learning specification. The findings suggest that preserving temporal information and effectively selecting relevant predictors are more important for accurate inflation nowcasting than increasing model complexity. The study highlights Google Trends as a timely complementary information source for inflation monitoring in India and demonstrates the importance of feature engineering in extracting economically meaningful signals from high-frequency search data.

detail.abstract:
Calendar seasonality — the claim that a given asset's returns are systematically higher or lower in
particular months, weeks, or days — is one of the oldest and most contested empirical regularities in
finance. This paper conducts two seasonality investigations in spot FX (EURUSD, GBPUSD, AUDUSD,
USDJPY), a market far less studied for calendar effects than equities, and reports both a
methodological cautionary tale and a substantive finding. We first document, as an opening case study,
a naive day-of-week/turn-of-month seasonality screen that not only fails on its own terms but
demonstrates — when retrofitted onto a near-miss intraday strategy from elsewhere in this series — a
concrete grid-design snooping mechanism: adding a five-level weekday filter as a free walk-forward
dimension causes a fold-level optimizer to chase noise and "discover" Monday as informative when, in
the full honest sample, Monday is in fact the worst-performing weekday. We then present a properly
designed successor study that trains an exact binomial sign test — the correct tool given only 2 to 8
yearly observations per calendar month, where a t-test's asymptotic assumptions do not remotely hold
— on rolling 2-, 5-, and 8-year trailing windows across the full symbol-month universe. Of 96 (symbol,
month, lookback) combinations tested, only four clear a defensible significance bar: EURUSD
February bearish, EURUSD and GBPUSD December bullish (a pattern independently corroborated by
well-documented year-end USD liquidity effects), and USDJPY June bullish. Pooling trades across all
four symbols, the resulting thin-sample backtest (13-18 trades per specification) shows that fading the
detected seasonal bias outperforms following it (expectancy +0.36R to +0.46R fading vs. -0.28R to
-0.40R following; permutation p ≈ 0.07-0.08) — the fourth independent instance, after the fibonacci-
pullback and liquidity-sweep/change-of-character findings reported in Papers 2 and 3 of this series, of
this research program's recurring meta-pattern that naive, textbook-obvious technical and calendar
narratives run backwards in this data. We connect this to the post-publication anomaly-decay
literature (McLean and Pontiff, 2016) and to overcrowded-positioning explanations for why a well-
advertised seasonal narrative might be more profitably faded than ridden. A supplementary exercise
applying the four identified biases since 2020 finds that a validated intraday timing signal (the
fibonacci-pullback-fade mechanism of Paper 2) restricted to fire only in the seasonally favored
direction outperforms naive buy-and-hold-the-season on two of three testable symbols, suggesting
seasonality is best treated as a directional filter layered onto a validated timing mechanism rather than
as a standalone strategy. We are explicit throughout that the sign-test detection finding and the
tradeability finding carry different confidence levels: the former is a correctly conducted, if modest,
statistical detection; the latter remains a suggestive, underpowered addendum.

title: Building Consulting and Coaching Psychology in India: A Scientist-practitioner Roadmap for Professionalisation

detail.title: Building Consulting and Coaching Psychology in India: A Scientist-practitioner Roadmap for Professionalisation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicting interests to declare

detail.abstract: Consulting psychology and coaching psychology are growing areas of applied psychological practice. Yet their institutionalisation remains uneven across countries and regions. This conceptual article, based on a critical analysis of literature and policy documents, examines the development of these fields in India. It argues that existing activities labelled management consulting, organisational development, and life coaching do not constitute a coherent professional system with consistently defined competencies, supervision, referral, or accountability mechanisms. Drawing on literature concerning consulting psychology, coaching psychology, professionalisation, psychology education, and regulation practices, the article proposes a staged roadmap for the development of the two disciplines in India. The roadmap addresses disciplinary boundaries, scientist-practitioner training, supervised practice and continuing professional development, ethical standards, confidentiality, assessment, and referral. The need for a professional society, the importance of locally grounded research, and longer-term statutory recognition are also emphasised. The article identifies challenges to the implementation of these and offers potential solutions. A brief research agenda is also presented. India is presented as a case study for examining culturally responsive development of consulting and coaching psychology in the Global South.

title: Cross-Section Estimation of Long-Run Relations Using Time-Compressed Data
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Economics and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta

detail.title: Cross-Section Estimation of Long-Run Relations Using Time-Compressed Data
detail.abstract:
Many empirical investigations of long-run relations are based on cross-section regressions in averaged or long differenced data that effectively have the time dimension of a T × N panel compressed. We analyze a class of time-compressed I(1) data and show that they have magnified variability stemming from the fact that the cross-section variance of a non-stationary panel ‘fans out’ with time. Cross-section regressions in time compressed data can potentially yield estimates that are super-consistent and asymptotically normal, whether the regressors are stationary, non-stationary, or highly persistent. The fastest convergence rate of √NT requires a compression scheme that not only magnifies the non-stationary signal, but also dilutes the regression noise. Omitted fixed effects preclude noise dilution but the estimates remain superconsistent. However, the fanning out effect can be weakened when the data have a strong force for mean-reversion or convergence, a problem that seems relevant for temperature data. We consider three applications and find that the long-run relation between consumption and income, and between growth/inflation and demographic variables are reasonably well determined, but the estimated relation between growth and warming temperature is fragile.

detail.abstract:
We test whether two widely-followed, publicly available sources of currency-market information — positioning data from
the CFTC's Commitment of Traders (COT) reports and interest-rate differentials underlying the carry trade — generate
tradeable out-of-sample edge in four major currency pairs (EUR, GBP, JPY, AUD vs. USD), after realistic transaction costs
and under an anchored walk-forward/holdout protocol with deflated-Sharpe multiple-testing correction. Study 1 tests six
distinct, professionally documented ways of reading COT data — a raw z-score of positioning level, the practitioner "COT
Index," week-over-week positioning flow, percent-of-open-interest, a small-trader fade, and the classic Legacy Commercial
("smart money") read — pooled across the four currencies, on daily bars, with a conservative five-calendar-day release-lag
buffer to avoid look-ahead. All six converge on the same clean negative result: no methodology clears permutation
significance (best p = 0.549), no methodology's deflated Sharpe ratio exceeds 0.00, and no methodology satisfies this
project's joint validation bar of out-of-sample significance, holdout agreement, and walk-forward stability together. Study 2
tests the classical uncovered-interest-parity carry trade using real FRED policy-rate differentials — not an academic proxy
or a broker's current swap quote — across the same four pairs individually and as an equal-weight portfolio. Every
configuration is a clean negative after costs (best out-of-sample Sharpe: -0.25), yet four of five configurations' walk-forward
optimizer, with no economic prior imposed, independently selected the theoretically correct sign of the trade (long the
higher-yielding currency) — the first time in this eleven-paper research program's history that a free-direction parameter
has converged on a coherent, theory-consistent answer rather than flip-flopping. We interpret the contrast between these
two studies and this series' single validated finding (structural price divergence, Paper 4 of this series) as informative about
where exploitable information plausibly still resides in this dataset: not in slow-moving, publicly disseminated survey and
macro data that the efficient-markets hypothesis predicts should already be priced in, but potentially in faster, structurally-
revealed features of price itself.

title: Beyond the Smokestack: Supply Chains and the Industrial Incidence of Net Zero
affiliations: University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne),  and Ecole Polytechnique, Palaiseau

detail.title: Beyond the Smokestack: Supply Chains and the Industrial Incidence of Net Zero
detail.abstract: We study the industrial incidence of net zero in DICE-IO, a 33-sector climateeconomy model calibrated to global input-output data. The standard smokestack principle suggests that the largest direct emitters should bear the largest transition burden. We show that this incidence logic breaks down in a production network: carbon costs propagate downstream and can weigh most heavily on industries that use carbon-intensive inputs. We summarize this mechanism with a sufficient statistic for first-order price incidence, the Leontief-based embodied-emissions multiplier, which we call Downstream Emission Centrality (DEC). DEC equals the sectoral price response to a marginal Scope-1 carbon tax and explains nearly all cross-sectional price variation along the nonlinear net-zero transition. Achieving the Paris Agreement target requires a carbon tax rising to about $1,300 per ton of CO 2 by 2050. The Scope-1 transition has a consumption-equivalent welfare cost of 0.7% relative to laissez-faire, while a Scope-3-style tax on embodied carbon in purchases yields a welfare gain of 1.1%.

detail.abstract: We experimentally examine how time blocking (dividing a fixed work period into shorter intervals) and non-binding goals influence worker performance. Measuring four outcomes, task performance, effort, accuracy, and mistake rate, we find that time blocking primarily operates through a speed accuracy trade off. While it substantially increases the number of tables attempted within a given period it simultaneously reduces accuracy, resulting in only a modest net gain in output. Goal setting, meanwhile, has no significant effect overall. The effects are heterogeneous and depend strongly on worker ability. For high-ability workers, goal setting significantly improves performance. Combining time blocking with goal setting yields the largest performance gains, indicating that the two techniques complement each other for this group. For low-ability workers, neither technique, individually or combined, produces significant improvements: although time blocking raises effort, the associated decline in accuracy offsets any potential benefit. Our findings highlight worker ability as a key moderator of non-monetary motivational interventions and caution against applying multiple techniques simultaneously without accounting for workforce heterogeneity.

detail.abstract: Measured real-exchange-rate persistence depends on both the speed of adjustment and the equilibrium towards which adjustment occurs. We examine these dimensions jointly using five US-dollar real exchange rates-sterling, the French franc, the Japanese yen, and the Australian and Canadian dollars-over samples extending for as long as two centuries. The long span supplies both power against slow reversion and the cumulative productivity variation needed to identify a moving equilibrium. Pair-specific evidence distinguishes linear from nonlinear reversion and allows the equilibrium real rate to move with relative productivity, as implied by the Harrod-Balassa-Samuelson (HBS) mechanism. Sterling, the franc and the yen display reversion in the maintained nonlinear equations. The Australian dollar reverts linearly, while the Canadian dollar supplies no sufficiently robust evidence of reversion. For the three nonlinear rates we estimate bilateral error-correction equations by Gaussian quasi-maximum likelihood and use bootstrap inference. The long-run productivity anchor is nearly one-for-one for the yen, positive and economically sizeable for the franc, and positive but more modest for sterling. Contemporaneous productivity pass-through is small, and equality between the short-and long-run productivity coefficients is rejected for the franc and the yen but not for sterling. Allowing the equilibrium to follow the productivity differential reduces the yen's implied linear half-life from 16.5 years to 2.8. History-conditioned nonlinear responses show that larger disequilibria generally correct faster. The cross-currency evidence is therefore selective: HBS drift matters greatly where relative productivity moves substantially, whereas constant parity remains the better empirical centre where it does not.

detail.abstract: Regenerative endodontic therapy (RET) has emerged as a biologically based treatment for necrotic immature permanent teeth, aiming to restore a functional pulp-dentin complex while promoting continued root development and periapical healing. Successful RET relies heavily on effective root canal disinfection, with irrigation serving as the primary method for reducing microbial load while preserving the viability of stem cells from the apical papilla and the integrity of the dentin matrix. Unlike conventional root canal treatment, RET requires irrigation protocols that achieve antimicrobial efficacy without compromising stem cell survival or the release of bioactive growth factors essential for tissue regeneration. This narrative review evaluates current evidence regarding irrigation strategies used in RET through a comprehensive analysis of published experimental, preclinical, and clinical studies. Major irrigants discussed include sodium hypochlorite, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), chlorhexidine, and emerging adjunctive solutions. The evidence indicates that low-concentration sodium hypochlorite followed by a final rinse with 17% EDTA provides an optimal balance between disinfection and preservation of the regenerative microenvironment. Appropriate irrigation protocols enhance stem cell viability, facilitate growth factor release, and improve clinical outcomes. Future research should focus on developing novel bioactive irrigants, standardized clinical protocols, and long-term randomized clinical trials to further optimize regenerative outcomes and establish evidence-based guidelines for RET.

detail.abstract: This article analyses the structural transformation of European retail banking driven by Online Deposit Platforms (ODPs), intermediaries classified by the European Banking Authority as "comparison plus" platforms that dismantle traditional geographic and administrative frictions. While ODPs offer smaller credit institutions, such as Maltese Less Significant Institutions, a vital strategic mechanism to access deep foreign retail liquidity without physical branch networks, they fundamentally alter the underlying behavioural profile of retail liabilities. By converting granular retail savings into highly rate-sensitive balances, ODPs impart to these deposits the velocity and volatility typically associated with short-term wholesale funding. Consequently, existing micro prudential frameworks raise questions as to whether standard runoff assumptions always capture the behavioural characteristics of platform-mediated deposits under conditions of stress. Furthermore, layered intermediation models, such as fiduciary "For Benefit Of" omnibus accounts, obscure depositor visibility, fragment compliance responsibilities like Customer Due Diligence and Suspicious Activity Reporting across multiple entities, and heighten exposure to financial crime and cross-border regulatory arbitrage. To reconcile the disconnect between nominal legal classifications and actual systemic risk, European regulatory authorities must transition from traditional entity centric models towards an activity-based supervisory paradigm.

title: Do Sources and Frames Improve Responses to Vaccine Misinformation Corrections? Evidence from a Randomized Survey Experiment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Seoul National University - Graduate School of Public Health

detail.title: Do Sources and Frames Improve Responses to Vaccine Misinformation Corrections? Evidence from a Randomized Survey Experiment
detail.abstract: Vaccine misinformation can undermine confidence not only in individual vaccines but also in their concurrent administration. We conducted a randomized online survey experiment among Korean adults (N=2,623) to examine what matters most in misinformation correction: the factual rebuttal itself, who delivers it, or how it is framed. Participants were assigned to misinformation-only exposure or one of 15 corrective-message conditions varying in institutional attribution and persuasive framing. Outcomes were perceived factuality, message trust, perceived usefulness, and perceived influence on vaccination intention.,We distinguished overall responses to corrective-message conditions relative to misinformation-only exposure from incremental effects relative to an unattributed fact-only condition. All corrective-message conditions produced positive total effects across the four outcomes. The fact-only correction increased perceived factuality and trust by 38.3 percentage points, usefulness by 39.0 points, and the probability of reporting influence on vaccination intention by 43.1 points (all p<.001). Additional source attribution or framing did not uniformly improve responses beyond factual correction, although selected framing conditions and source–frame combinations improved factuality, trust, or usefulness. No augmented correction significantly differed from the fact-only correction in perceived influence on vaccination intention.,Factual corrective information produced the broadest and most consistent favorable immediate responses, whereas source attribution and framing provided selective, outcome-specific benefits. Vaccine communication should prioritize clear factual correction and use messenger and framing choices strategically. Perceived influence on vaccination intention should not be interpreted as a directional change in intention or vaccination behavior.

title: Nothing to See Here: Judicial Sanewashing and the Obfuscation of Constitutional Disorder

detail.abstract:
Less than two years after critics cautioned of the dystopian results of “sanewashing” Donald Trump’s incoherent and factually untethered public pronouncements during the 2024 presidential elections, the country’s political and legal landscape has become unrecognizable. The federal government is engaged in a coordinated campaign of racial and ethnic profiling, endorsed by the Supreme Court.  Paramilitary government forces of masked men openly hunt immigrants and terrorize American cities.  Public executions of unarmed citizens, captured on video for all to see, are refuted by government officials as legally justifiable and entitled to absolute immunity. The notion that we are a nation of laws, rather than of men, is increasingly difficult to defend.

The question is, how did we arrive here? How did basic due process protections, the rule of law, and an established system of checks and balances crumble so quickly and so spectacularly?  The answer to that question is “judicial sanewashing."  We need only look to the Roberts Court and its sanewashed treatment of law and facts to see how the United States evolved from a nation of laws into a sanewashed system predicated on legal, political, and factual distortions.

This article builds on an earlier piece examining the concept of “judicial sanewashing,” a term used to describe a growing phenomenon in which the Roberts Court relies on contrived interpretive methods and legal standards to radically rewrite the law and distort the true effects of its judicial decisions. Building upon the theoretical and taxonomical foundation set out in the first article, I now attempt to concretize the concept by examining the effects of judicial sanewashing techniques across several discrete but interrelated (and far from exhaustive) areas of the Supreme Court’s sanewashed jurisprudence. This article examines the effects of judicial sanewashing, drawing upon case illustrations from the Court’s rapidly evolving jurisprudence with respect to the weakening of political and civil rights for disfavored groups, the erosion of separation of powers, and the expansion of executive power under the Trump regime. In this article, I also explore the particularly destructive convergence of sanewashing, whitewashing, and mansplaining.

detail.abstract: As investors increasingly turn to generative AI (GenAI) to help process financial information and guide investment decisions, their investment position information is likely to enter GenAI's context window. Across three sets of experiments using GenAI as our subject in financial information processing settings, we predict and find that GenAI output is, on average, more positive when its context window indicates a long rather than short position. This investment position effect holds for both information evaluation and retrieval tasks. Further testing indicates the effect arises from GenAI shifting weight between positive and negative information in the context window. Consistent with this mechanism, the effect is strongest when the financial information contains a more balanced mix of positive and negative information and weakest when the information is more one-sided in valence. The effect is absent when only a single piece of information is provided, eliminating the opportunity to shift weight between positive and negative information. We also find that the effect persists after increasing the model's reasoning and after implementing simple prompt-based mitigation strategies. Together, our findings demonstrate how, when, and why subtle changes in GenAI's context window-including information about the user-can systematically shift how GenAI processes financial information.

title: Connectivage: A Historical Periodization for the Age of Communication, Information, and Artificial Intelligence: The End of the Contemporary and the Birth of Connectivage

detail.abstract:
This book proposes Connectivage as a historiographical category for understanding the long-term transformation of human societies through changes in the material conditions of communication, information circulation, and access to knowledge. Rather than treating historical periods as fixed or natural divisions, the work understands periodization as a heuristic instrument that organizes complex processes around structural transformations. From this perspective, the transition from the Modern Age to Proto-Connectivage (1789–1844) and the subsequent emergence of Connectivage are interpreted through changes in the ways information could be recorded, transmitted, reproduced, and accessed.

The proposed period extends from the consolidation of electrical telegraphy in the nineteenth century to the historical caesura of 2020–2022. It is divided into four phases: the emergence of electrical communication (1844–1914); communication and total war (1914–1945); technological competition and globalization of communication (1945–1991); and digitalization and the democratization of knowledge (1991–2020). The central argument is that these phases constitute a continuous historical process characterized by the progressive reduction of the constraints imposed by geographical distance on communication and information circulation.

The book further argues that the period 2020–2022 may represent a compound historical caesura. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the incorporation of digital infrastructure into everyday social life, while the mass diffusion of generative artificial intelligence, particularly following the public release of ChatGPT in 2022, introduced a qualitatively different function: artificial systems could increasingly participate in the generation, synthesis, transformation, classification, and organization of information. This transformation may have consequences comparable, in structural significance, to those produced by industrialization, particularly through the reorganization of work, intellectual production, and social relations.

On this basis, the book proposes the New Contemporary as a provisional designation for the historical present following the caesura. The concept is intentionally open to revision by future historians. The work concludes by outlining new possibilities for historiographical practice, including algorithmic source criticism, digital provenance, large-scale corpus analysis, interdisciplinary evidence integration, and methodologically controlled uses of artificial intelligence.

title: Bringing post-growth policy proposals to life: the role of law
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Bringing post-growth policy proposals to life: the role of law
detail.abstract: As an alternative to green growth strategies, the rapidly expanding field of post-growth research aims to transform socioeconomic systems to improve well-being while respecting planetary boundaries, without relying on growth. To enable such a change on a large scale through policy-making, post-growth researchers have put forward various policy proposals. Yet, their engagement with the role of law in bringing them to life remains limited. We argue that this is a fundamental shortcoming since policy proposals must be incorporated into legal systems to become binding. To identify the steps needed for better integrating law into post-growth policy proposals, we assessed how law has been considered thus far in relation to these proposals. To do so, we conducted two scoping reviews, one of non-legal post-growth research and the other of legal post-growth research. The results revealed a lack of integration between the two research fields. Non-legal scholars inconsistently acknowledge the distinct importance of the legal feasibility of post-growth policy proposals. They also rarely engage with the law from the perspective of its internal logic and do not typically approach legal sources holistically. In parallel, legal scholars seldom give post-growth policy proposals significant weight in their legal analysis. Moving forward, we argue that existing policy proposals should be jointly refined by non-legal and legal scholars in accordance with complex-adaptive characteristics of legal systems. They should be legally feasible, better grounded in existing legal systems and designed to target leverage points that can set change in motion at the level of foundational legal structures.

detail.abstract: Electrifying the energy market contributes to United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 7 (affordable and clean energy) and 13 (climate action), but it comes with unique challenges. Focusing on Australia as an example of a highly electrified market – world-leading in rooftop solar photovoltaic systems – we analyse smart-metered household electricity consumption in the state of Queensland to identify five distinct household electricity use patterns. We then assign 366,439,750 use days of 1,097,125 households to those patterns to derive household market segments with distinct electricity use and socio-demographic characteristics. Segment profiles show that the benefits of rooftop photovoltaics are asymmetrically leveraged by the population. Households with photovoltaic systems and daytime valley use typically live in their own house and report a high education and income level. Households without photovoltaics and consistent electricity use all day buy most electricity from the grid; they are more likely to rent, live in apartments and report lower income and education levels. Regulatory modifications can make the cost-saving benefits of solar systems available to a wider section of the community, while also contributing to carbon emissions reduction via an increase in renewable energy.

detail.abstract: Advocates for health equity frequently point to telemedicine as a promising way to achieve greater health access, and by extension, equity. This viewpoint, however, often fails to account for the ways in which the increased use of telemedicine-if accompanied by fraud-could adversely impact health equity. This article argues that while telehealth is an important tool in achieving health equity, the fraud-related risks that come along with that potential need to be examined. It does not argue against telemedicine as a potential path to achieving greater health equity; rather it simply notes the fraud-related risks that it comes with and highlights some efforts to address those risks.

title: A Good Name Matters: CEO Reputation and Corporate AI Washing

detail.title: A Good Name Matters: CEO Reputation and Corporate AI Washing
detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of AI has created unprecedented opportunities while also giving rise to AI washing. Such practices may undermine the sustainable development of the AI industry, highlighting the need for effective governance. Using data of Chinese A-share listed firms, this paper examines the impact of CEO reputation on corporate AI washing. We found that CEO reputation can curbs corporate AI washing by alleviating financing constraints and strengthening firms’ dynamic capabilities. Moreover, the effect is further reinforced by merchant guild culture and Confucian culture. Further analysis indicates that the governance effect of CEO reputation on corporate AI washing has persistence and spillover effects. CEO reputation also improves accounting conservatism and innovation efficiency. This study contributes to the literature on the firm-level consequences of CEO reputation by uncovering the drivers and governance mechanisms of corporate AI washing. It also offers practical implications for all sectors of society in addressing AI washing.

detail.abstract:
Background: Cancer is the leading cause of death in South Korea, yet five-year survival improved from below 50% in 2000 to 71.7% in 2020. The economic value of this mortality reduction has not been quantified using a nationally representative willingness-to-pay framework. We estimated the economic gains from reduced cancer mortality in South Korea between 2000 and 2020, and the prospective value of a further 1% reduction in cancer deaths.

Methods: We adapted the Murphy and Topel value-of-statistical-life (VSL) framework to a discrete-time model suited to Korean annual data. Age- and sex-specific values of a life-year were estimated from the 2020 Employment by Type of Work Survey and rescaled to 2000–2019 using per-capita GDP ratios. Age-specific cancer mortality rates were drawn from the Causes of Death Statistics (Statistics Korea). The aggregate value of mortality reductions was computed by multiplying age-specific gains in the value of remaining life by population counts.

Findings: The value of a life-year peaked at $155,000 around age 50 for men and $99,000 around age 35 for women; the value of remaining life reached $3.5 million and $2.5 million, respectively. Reductions in cancer mortality between 2000 and 2020 generated cumulative gains of approximately $11.9 trillion (2020 USD), averaging $595 billion per year—roughly one-third of annual GDP. A prospective 1% reduction in cancer mortality would yield an estimated $27 billion.

Interpretation: Sustained investment in cancer control has produced economic returns far exceeding its cost, supporting continued prioritisation of cancer research and care in national health policy.

title: FROM IMPORTER TO SUPPLIER: HOW AGGREGATE CLEAN-ENERGY TRADE STATISTICS CONCEAL A STAGE-SPECIFIC REVERSAL -- EVIDENCE FROM CHINA'S RENEWABLE TRANSITION
affiliations: Korea University and Korea University

detail.title: FROM IMPORTER TO SUPPLIER: HOW AGGREGATE CLEAN-ENERGY TRADE STATISTICS CONCEAL A STAGE-SPECIFIC REVERSAL -- EVIDENCE FROM CHINA'S RENEWABLE TRANSITION
detail.abstract: Aggregate clean-energy trade can show little country-specific change even when a country moves from importing the equipment that generates renewable electricity to supplying that equipment abroad. We study this possibility during China's mid-2000s renewable-energy transition using bilateral trade data for 2002--2010. We compare changes in China's imports and exports with changes in the same products across other countries. For 21 renewable-related products, China's import and export changes are close to international trends. We then separate these products into upstream materials, intermediate components and electrical equipment, and generation equipment that converts wind, water, or sunlight into electricity. At the generation-equipment stage, China's import intensity falls by about 45 percent relative to other importers, while its export specialization rises by about 156 percent relative to other exporters. China moves from a USD 0.41 billion net importer of these products in 2005 to a USD 19.79 billion net exporter in 2010. We also quantify China's contribution to the international import benchmark. Chinese shipments account for 42.2 percent of the increase in other countries' generation-equipment purchases; removing them still leaves a 38 percent relative import decline. The pattern remains for wind and hydropower equipment when the solar photovoltaic-related product is reassigned to the comparison group, and the export result remains large within the same destination, product, and year. Total clean-energy trade is therefore an incomplete measure of reliance on foreign generation equipment. Energy-transition supply-chain assessments should report generation equipment separately from materials and intermediate goods.

title: Driving change: Heterogeneous effects of electric vehicle adoption on travel behavior
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, CPB Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Driving change: Heterogeneous effects of electric vehicle adoption on travel behavior
detail.abstract: Electric vehicles (EVs) eliminate tailpipe emissions, but their lower marginal cost of driving may induce additional car travel, possibly at the expense of other modes. We estimate the effect of vehicle electrification on travel behavior, linking trip-level data from the 2023 Dutch National Travel Survey to administrative microdata on individuals, households and vehicle registrations through 2025. To address selection into EV adoption, we compare contemporaneous EV adopters with not-yet-adopters: households that hold only combustion vehicles at the survey date but acquire an EV within the following one to two years. EV adoption increases car kilometers with no significant change in the number of car trips, indicating longer or chained trips rather than more frequent ones. The response is markedly heterogeneous: additional driving concentrates on weekends, off-peak hours and non-commuting trips, and among households in densely populated areas. We find no evidence that EV adoption displaces cycling or walking; estimates for public transport are too imprecise to be conclusive. The heterogeneous effects of EV adoption on travel behavior have implications for transport and infrastructure policies, including road pricing and accessibility investments.

title: Exploring the Motivations and Perceptions Behind Skin Bleaching Practices Among Men and Women
affiliations: University of Dschang, University of Yaounde II and University of Dschang

detail.title: Exploring the Motivations and Perceptions Behind Skin Bleaching Practices Among Men and Women
detail.abstract: Skin bleaching is a widespread practice across many cultures, often linked to societal ideals that favor lighter skin tones, with high prevalence in Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean. This study investigates the perceptions and motivations behind bleaching among cosmetic consumers using a cross-sectional survey of 549 respondents, comprising 64.66% women and 35.34% men. Results indicate that physical attractiveness, being beautiful or handsome is the primary motive driving bleaching behaviors, though gendered differences emerge. Women are more strongly influenced by peer pressure and partners, while advertising significantly correlates with cosmetic product consumption across both sexes. The findings challenge the long-standing perception that cosmetics and bleaching are primarily female-oriented by revealing men’s active engagement in the practice and their exposure to similar social and marketing pressures. This contribution extends consumer and cosmetic studies into an underexplored area of inquiry and provides new insights into the cultural and psychological dimensions of bleaching behaviors. Nevertheless, the study is not without limitations. Its cross-sectional design captures attitudes at only one point in time, limiting the ability to track behavioral changes. Reliance on self-reported data raises the possibility of bias of social desirability, while the geographically restricted sample constrains generalizability across diverse cultural contexts. Furthermore, the exclusive focus on cosmetic consumers may overlook deeper motivations tied to culture, identity, or historical factors. Despite these limitations, this study offers valuable evidence on the complex drivers of skin bleaching and underscores the need for longitudinal and qualitative research to better capture its evolving dynamics.

title: Female Micro-Entrepreneurship and Child Development
affiliations: Brown University - Department of Economics, Rice University and Washington University in St. Louis - Department of Economics

detail.title: Female Micro-Entrepreneurship and Child Development
detail.abstract: Ultra-poor graduation programs (UPG) reliably reduce extreme poverty among adult recipients, yet their intergenerational effects on children remain largely undocumented. We study a child-focused UPG in rural Malawi that augments the standard graduation bundle with early childhood development (ECD) training, targeting mothers with young children in a population that is both severely stunted and approximately 1 SD behind international benchmarks on cognitive and non-cognitive development. In an RCT of 1,872 households, we show that the intervention raises child development by 0.16 to 0.26 SD within one year but has no significant effects on anthropometrics. Behind the impacts is a broad shift in parental inputs and behaviors. The results demonstrate that a child-focused anti-poverty program can generate child development gains that have not been documented in comparable programs without a child focus.
